complaisant.meaning: Someone complaisant says yes and goes along with you rather than standing their ground.
complaisant.clue: Our new assistant always smiled and agreed with the manager's plans, even when she privately thought them foolish.

complex.meaning: A complex idea has lots of different parts, which makes it hard to explain quickly.
complex.clue: The instructions for that model kit were so hard to follow that we spent an hour finding the first piece.

complicity.meaning: Complicity means being a part of wrongdoing because you helped someone else do it.
complicity.clue: The driver who handed over the keys had helped plan the theft from the very beginning.

component.meaning: A component is one small section of something much bigger that it depends on.
component.clue: The engineer checked every single section of the engine, since the car cannot run if even one is broken.

composed.meaning: Someone composed keeps cool and does not panic when things go wrong.
composed.clue: When the power failed in the hall, the headteacher kept her voice steady and told everyone what to do.

composure.meaning: Composure is the calm that lets you think clearly during a frightening moment.
composure.clue: Despite the noise and the flashing lights, the driver kept her nerve and brought everyone to safety.

comprehend.meaning: To comprehend something is to take in its full meaning, not just the surface words.
comprehend.clue: Even after reading it three times, I still could not see what the writer meant by that last sentence.

conceive.meaning: To conceive a plan is to form it in your head before anyone else hears of it.
conceive.clue: She dreamed up an idea for a recycling scheme, and the council agreed to pay for it.

concentrated.meaning: When you are concentrated, one job fills your whole mind and other things fade.
concentrated.clue: He gave all his attention to the model bridge, ignoring the noise of the crowded room.

concerted.meaning: A concerted effort is one that a group plans carefully together from the start.
concerted.clue: It took a planned effort by the whole staff to finish the school show on time.

conciliatory.meaning: A conciliatory gesture aims to end a quarrel rather than win the argument.
conciliatory.clue: He smiled, said sorry and offered to share his sweets, so the class soon stopped whispering.

concise.meaning: A concise answer says everything that matters in as few words as possible.
concise.clue: His reply was so short that we still do not know what the coach wants us to do.

conclude.meaning: To conclude a meeting is to close it and usually make a final decision.
conclude.clue: After two hours of talking about the trip, the headteacher made her final decision and let everyone go home.

conclusive.meaning: When the evidence is conclusive, there is no room left for doubt about the answer.
conclusive.clue: The photographs were conclusive proof that our team had won, so nobody could argue with the result.

concoct.meaning: Someone who concocts a tale is making it up rather than telling the truth.
concoct.clue: Sam managed to concoct an extraordinary excuse for missing his homework, but his teacher was not fooled for a second.

condescension.meaning: Condescension is the sort of behaviour that makes other people feel small and unimportant.
condescension.clue: Her teacher disliked her condescension towards the younger pupils and asked her to treat them with kindness instead.

condone.meaning: To condone something is to let it happen even though you know it is wrong.
condone.clue: The head teacher refused to condone the children throwing rubbish in the corridor, and told them to clear it up.

conducive.meaning: A quiet room is conducive to study because nothing in it distracts you from your work.
conducive.clue: A tidy, well-lit desk is conducive to good handwriting, so our teacher always clears the space before we start.

confer.meaning: When a group confers, they meet to talk something over and decide what to do.
confer.clue: The head teacher invited the school council to confer with her about the new playground rules before the vote.

conferred.meaning: After the two sides had conferred, everyone knew exactly what had been agreed.
conferred.clue: After the two head teachers conferred at breakfast, they agreed to share one set of sports kit.

confide.meaning: When you confide in someone, you trust them enough to share your worries with them.
confide.clue: She confided in her best friend that she was nervous about the secondary school interview, which helped her relax.

confine.meaning: The children were confined to the hall until the broken ceiling could be repaired.
confine.clue: During the exam, candidates must confine their writing to the box marked on the front of the paper.

confiscate.meaning: The confiscated phone was given back to its owner once the lesson had finished.
confiscate.clue: Our teacher will confiscate any phone that rings during the lesson, so please switch yours off before you sit down.

confound.meaning: A hard sum like that confounded me, and I could not work out the answer at all.
confound.clue: The hardest question confounded everyone, and half the class carried on writing even after the bell rang.

congenial.meaning: A congenial host makes you feel welcome and comfortable the moment you arrive.
congenial.clue: Our new head teacher is so congenial that even the shy pupils ask her questions at break time.

congested.meaning: A congested road means long queues of cars moving very slowly, often near a junction.
congested.clue: By eight o'clock the road outside school is so congested that we are often ten minutes late for registration.

connoisseur.meaning: A connoisseur can tell a genuine old painting from a very clever copy.
connoisseur.clue: My uncle is a real connoisseur of jazz, and he can name the band playing from just three notes.

consensus.meaning: A consensus means the group settles on one answer that everyone is willing to support.
consensus.clue: After a long talk about the trip, the class reached a consensus and chose the museum instead of the cinema.

consent.meaning: Nobody may enter the laboratory without the consent of the teacher in charge of it.
consent.clue: The school needs parental consent before any pupil may take part in the visit to France next July.

conservation.meaning: Water conservation means taking shorter showers and turning off the tap while brushing your teeth.
conservation.clue: Our school holds a conservation week so that pupils learn how little water and electricity we really need.

consideration.meaning: After considering the risks, the head teacher gave the trip the go-ahead.
consideration.clue: The committee gave the proposal serious consideration before agreeing that the sports day should go ahead.

consistency.meaning: Consistency matters in music practice: playing a little every day beats one long session before the exam.
consistency.clue: His marking shows real consistency: every essay he writes is neatly laid out and fully finished.

conspire.meaning: Two classmates conspired to cheat, but their plan fell apart when the teacher moved their desks.
conspire.clue: The two brothers conspired to give their mother a fake present, and hid the wrapping paper under the stairs.

constant.meaning: Since he began the medicine, the constant headache in the afternoon has completely gone.
constant.clue: There was constant chatter in the corridor before the bell, and the teacher looked quite cross.

constrain.meaning: Bad weather constrained the coach driver, so the team only travelled thirty miles that day.
constrain.clue: Our teacher constrained the length of each essay to one page, so nobody could ramble forever.

constraint.meaning: The constraint that no mobile phones may be used in the hall upset a few of the older pupils.
constraint.clue: One real constraint on our project is money, as the school will only pay for the materials.

construe.meaning: His silence was construed as a yes, although he had really meant something else entirely.
construe.clue: Some pupils construed my joking comment about the exam as a serious warning.

consume.meaning: Running the heating all day consumed most of the gas in the tank before the winter was over.
consume.clue: Our class has consumed three whole packets of biscuits waiting for the weather to improve.

contagious.meaning: Chickenpox is highly contagious, so my brother was told to stay at home for a week.
contagious.clue: By Friday the cough had proved contagious, and our form tutor sent three of us home early.

contemptuous.meaning: He gave me a contemptuous look when I asked a simple question about the lesson.
contemptuous.clue: Several fans were contemptuous of the referee, believing the second goal should have been ruled out.

contend.meaning: My brother contends that football is boring, and he makes sure we never watch it together.
contend.clue: The two pupils contended fiercely for the last biscuit until the teacher stepped in and broke it.

content.meaning: With a hot meal and a warm room, he was perfectly content to stay in and read.
content.clue: We were quite content to walk instead of paying for a taxi, and saved enough for a hot drink.

contentious.meaning: Housing where the school is built is always contentious, and local people argued about it for months.
contentious.clue: Moving the footpath across the field proved contentious, so the council held three public meetings.

contest.meaning: The spelling bee was such a fun contest that even the teachers entered their names.
contest.clue: Our house team won the quiz contest by three points, and everyone cheered for the whole of assembly.

contorted.meaning: The contorted metal sculpture in the town square looks like a giant wave frozen in time.
contorted.clue: He made such a contorted face when the unexpected visitor walked in that we all burst out laughing.

contract.meaning: Both schools signed the contract, so the coach will bring the pupils home at four o'clock.
contract.clue: Our group read every clause of the contract before signing, because our parents had to agree too.

contradict.meaning: His later message contradicted what he had said the day before, and nobody could believe either version.
contradict.clue: The two boys' stories contradicted each other, so the teacher asked the whole class to stay calm.

contribute.meaning: Everyone contributed something towards the school play, from costumes to biscuits for the audience.
contribute.clue: She contributed a huge box of biscuits to the bring-and-buy sale and raised money for the animal shelter.

contrite.meaning: He was contrite after breaking the window, and offered to pay for a new one straight away.
contrite.clue: A pupil who admits being wrong without making excuses is showing a contrite attitude, which a teacher always respects.

contrition.meaning: His contrition was obvious from the moment he offered to return the money without being asked.
contrition.clue: She showed real contrition by writing to the pupil she had upset and asking to be friends again.

contrived.meaning: The show of friendship was contrived, because every word of the apology had been planned in advance.
contrived.clue: His excuse for forgetting his book was so contrived that nobody in the class believed a word of it.

conundrum.meaning: How the school timetable works is a real conundrum, and nobody seems to know who makes it.
conundrum.clue: Why the old pipes leak only in winter is such a conundrum that even the caretaker cannot explain it.

convenient.meaning: The new bus stop on the corner is very convenient, saving us a ten-minute walk every morning.
convenient.clue: It was convenient to finish our science experiment early, so we used the spare lesson to tidy the lab.

convert.meaning: The old mill has been converted into flats, but the brick windows were left exactly as they were.
convert.clue: We converted an old shed at the bottom of the garden into a workshop for making models.

convey.meaning: The advert conveys the idea of fun without saying a single word about the actual price.
convey.clue: A picture can convey an idea to someone who cannot read very well, which is why our posters include symbols.

conveyor.meaning: The bottles travel along a conveyor from the lorry to the fridge in seconds.
conveyor.clue: A conveyor moved the hundreds of packed lunches along, and each of us took one as it went past.

convict.meaning: The photographs finally helped to convict him, and the court agreed that he had stolen the money.
convict.clue: Two shopkeepers said they saw the same man empty the register, which was enough to convict him in the end.

convince.meaning: The photographs convinced the police that the boy had not taken the money after all.
convince.clue: A good diagram convinced the class that the river changes course twice in one year.

convoluted.meaning: The instructions for the model plane were so convoluted that we had to ask for a second sheet.
convoluted.clue: His explanation of the rules was so convoluted that half of us gave up and copied someone else's notes.

copious.meaning: Copious rain in May filled the water butt, and we watered the plants all summer long.
copious.clue: The runner took copious notes during the talk, and afterwards she could answer every question.

corpse.meaning: Farmers sometimes find a sheep's corpse in a field, but they must always ring the vet.
corpse.clue: We had to turn away when the guide opened the case, because the shrivelled corpse inside was far worse than we expected.

corroborate.meaning: Two witnesses told the same story, which corroborated the boy's account of the fire.
corroborate.clue: Her measurements corroborated the report from the weather station, so the head teacher used her figures in the newsletter.

corrosive.meaning: Because the acid is highly corrosive, it is stored in a thick plastic tank.
corrosive.clue: The damp weather turned the railings rusty, and the council used a corrosive chemical to strip the old paint.

counterargument.meaning: The new point raises questions about an earlier claim and shows why it may be wrong.
counterargument.clue: Miss Ahmed asked us to offer a counterargument before the team started writing its final response.

courageous.meaning: You have to be courageous to stand up and say that an adult is wrong.
courageous.clue: The courageous pupil volunteered to read her poem aloud to the whole hall.

crass.meaning: Making fun of somebody who is upset shows a total lack of thought for others.
crass.clue: It was crass of him to laugh when the new pupil was still nervous on her very first day.

craving.meaning: She had a craving for the violin she had seen in the shop window.
craving.clue: After the concert, Sam felt a craving to play the piano his sister had left behind.

credence.meaning: Something is only worth listening to if there is real proof behind it.
credence.clue: Nobody gave credence to the rumour until the head teacher stood up and confirmed it.

credibility.meaning: A person who changes her story loses the right to be taken seriously.
credibility.clue: The young witness lost all her credibility after giving the police two different stories.

credible.meaning: The story has to sound reasonable, otherwise nobody will accept it as the truth.
credible.clue: At first the children invented a credible story about the noises they had heard in the corridor.

credit.meaning: She deserves credit for organising charity week all by herself.
credit.clue: The head teacher gave Tom credit for organising the charity week all by himself.

credulous.meaning: People were credulous enough to believe that a stranger had won the lottery.
credulous.clue: The young shoppers were credulous about the man outside the station offering free sweets.

creek.meaning: A shallow water channel like this one can be crossed safely at the ford.
creek.clue: We followed the creek down to the ford, then splashed across to reach the meadow.

criterion.meaning: Success in the exam was the main criterion for getting a place at the school.
criterion.clue: Getting to school on time was the criterion our class used for winning a place on the team.

crucial.meaning: Missing this one step means the whole plan falls apart.
crucial.clue: It is crucial to arrive by nine if you want a hot lunch on Thursday.

cryptic.meaning: The crossword clue was cryptic and only two boys solved it.
cryptic.clue: The new maths questions were so cryptic that half the class had to ask for help.

culpable.meaning: It seemed unfair to hold such a young pupil responsible for the damage.
culpable.clue: Nobody believed the youngest child was culpable for the broken window in the corridor.

cultivate.meaning: Good soil, careful work and the right seeds are all needed before a field will give a harvest.
cultivate.clue: Growers cultivate the strip of land beside the river to bring in a barley harvest each summer.

cumbersome.meaning: The new trolley was so cumbersome that we could not get it upstairs.
cumbersome.clue: We had to move the piano twice because the old box was so cumbersome to handle.

cunning.meaning: The cunning fox tricked the hens into opening the gate.
cunning.clue: That cunning sales assistant promised free tickets and then asked for a signature.

curate.meaning: She is responsible for deciding what goes into the show and in which order.
curate.clue: The pupil who will curate our museum display has already chosen the old photographs.

curb.meaning: Try to curb your excitement until the surprise party begins.
curb.clue: It is hard to curb your excitement when the class is told about the trip.

curious.meaning: She was always the first to ask why, rather than accepting what she was told.
curious.clue: The curious class crowded round the old robot and asked twenty questions about it.

cursory.meaning: He gave the chapter only a cursory glance before the bell rang.
cursory.clue: With exams tomorrow, a cursory look at the notes was never going to be enough.

custodian.meaning: Someone in this role checks the building and makes sure it stays secure.
custodian.clue: The custodian of the museum checks the alarms before the doors open each morning.

custom.meaning: It is custom in our house to leave our shoes in the hall.
custom.clue: It is custom at our school to shake hands with the head teacher each morning.

customary.meaning: This sort of thing happens here every single year without fail.
customary.clue: It was customary for our choir to sing at the end of every term.

cynic.meaning: The cynic in the story mocked everyone who tried to be kind.
cynic.clue: No one liked the cynic who laughed every time somebody offered to help.

dale.meaning: Long hollows like this one lie between the hills in the north of England.
dale.clue: The walk took us along a dale where sheep grazed quietly beside the stone walls.

daring.meaning: Not many people would have the nerve to try that in freezing water.
daring.clue: It was daring of you to swim in the cold river before breakfast on Saturday.

darn.meaning: Using a needle and wool like this can mend a hole perfectly well.
darn.clue: Grandma showed me how to darn the hole in the sleeve of my jumper.

daunt.meaning: A huge empty hall can be enough to shake your confidence completely.
daunt.clue: The huge exam hall and the rows of desks daunted Mia until her teacher smiled.

debacle.meaning: The whole school trip was a debacle after the coach broke down.
debacle.clue: The end-of-year trip became quite a debacle when the rain washed away the games.

debate.meaning: The class debate on homework lasted nearly an hour.
debate.clue: In the school debate, Priya argued well and Tom answered her points calmly.

debilitate.meaning: The long illness debilitated him, so he walked with a stick.
debilitate.clue: Months of illness debilitated Dad, and he needed a stick to walk to school.

debrief.meaning: The police debriefed the witnesses about the robbery.
debrief.clue: After the match, the coach called the players in to debrief them on their mistakes.

debris.meaning: Once a storm has brought trees down, the broken branches must be cleared away.
debris.clue: The council cleared the debris left on the road after the storm had brought down trees.

debunk.meaning: The article tries to debunk the myth that we swallow eight spiders a year.
debunk.clue: Our school project tried to debunk the story that hair grows back thicker after cutting.

decadent.meaning: When a society grows too rich and idle, it starts to rot from within.
decadent.clue: The film showed a decadent kingdom where the palace walls were gold and nobody worked.

decency.meaning: He showed decency by giving up his seat on the bus.
decency.clue: Asking the dinner lady how her day had been was a simple act of decency.

decipher.meaning: It took the whole class a week to decipher the coded message.
decipher.clue: With the help of a magnifying glass, Fatima tried to decipher the strange writing in the margin.

decisive.meaning: The captain had to be decisive when the match was nearly lost.
decisive.clue: The captain was decisive, telling the goalkeeper exactly where to send the ball.

declare.meaning: The results were read out to the whole hall at the end of the morning assembly.
declare.clue: The head teacher declared the results of the writing competition in front of the whole school.

decline.meaning: Once something is no longer sold in the shop, people buy far less of it.
decline.clue: Sales of fizzy drinks declined sharply after the shop stopped selling them at break time.

decorum.meaning: Shouting across the hall while others are talking is very badly behaved.
decorum.clue: There was no decorum at all while the new pupils shouted across the dining hall.

decree.meaning: An announcement from the ruler must be obeyed, whatever people think of it.
decree.clue: By royal decree, no heavy lorries may pass through the village square after dark.

deduce.meaning: Working backwards from the clues lets you reach the right answer.
deduce.clue: From the mud on her boots we deduced that Priya had already been in the garden.

defame.meaning: He was careful never to defame his neighbour in front of the whole street.
defame.clue: The newspaper refused to print the letter because it would defame an innocent family.

deference.meaning: Showing respect for an important visitor means waiting quietly for them.
deference.clue: The children showed deference by standing up immediately when the judge came into court.

defiance.meaning: The boys openly ignored the rule and showed they had no intention of obeying it.
defiance.clue: The pupils showed open defiance by refusing to hand in their confiscated mobile phones.

defunct.meaning: The old cannon in the courtyard has been defunct for over a century.
defunct.clue: The museum keeps a defunct printing press that was used in the town until 1985.

degenerate.meaning: When somebody's behaviour turns so bad, they lose the trust of everyone.
degenerate.clue: His degenerate behaviour in the queue cost him a place in the school team.

degrade.meaning: Rubbish left on the beach makes the whole shore less pleasant for everyone.
degrade.clue: Dumping old paint in the river would degrade the water and kill the fish.

deject.meaning: Losing the final left the whole team feeling low for days afterwards.
deject.clue: After the team lost the final, the disappointed players sat in silence while the coach tried to raise their spirits again.

delectable.meaning: The warm smell of baking bread made the whole street feel welcoming.
delectable.clue: We were given a plate of freshly baked scones, and their wonderful smell drew us to the kitchen at once.

delightful.meaning: The kind old man made our afternoon with his funny stories and warm smile.
delightful.clue: A gentle breeze came through the open window and the birdsong outside was so lovely that everyone smiled.

delineate.meaning: The report sets out clearly which changes will be made to the school buildings.
delineate.clue: The architect drew a careful plan of the new sports hall, showing exactly where every wall would stand.

delirious.meaning: When she heard the news, she jumped up and down and could not stop laughing.
delirious.clue: On hearing the surprise announcement, the pupils shouted, cheered and threw their hats in the air.

delude.meaning: The salesman tricked us into paying for a car that had been in a serious accident.
delude.clue: The salesman persuaded us that the used car was faultless, when in fact he had hidden its real problems.

deluge.meaning: After the storm, the whole road was flooded and buses could not get through.
deluge.clue: The storm arrived without warning, and within minutes the gutters overflowed and cars stood in deep water.

demeanour.meaning: She walked into the hall with a calm, confident way that impressed everyone.
demeanour.clue: Everyone noticed his calm, confident way of walking into the hall to meet the new headteacher.

demote.meaning: Although she was the most experienced, the new manager moved her to a junior post.
demote.clue: After the restructure, Mr Ali was given a smaller class, which many staff felt was a step backwards.

denounce.meaning: The whole class spoke out against the plan to close the library.
denounce.clue: At the public meeting, angry parents fiercely attacked the plan to sell the playing field.

deny.meaning: He said he had never taken the money, even though the camera had filmed him.
deny.clue: When the teacher asked who had eaten the biscuits, he flatly said that it had not been him.

depict.meaning: The opening chapter gives a vivid picture of village life in the 1920s.
depict.clue: In her diary, Amy captured the noisy playground in vivid detail, from the swings to the boys' football.

deplore.meaning: Everyone was upset when the announcement that the school would close was made.
deplore.clue: Residents filled the town hall to say how upset they were about the closure of the local hospital.

deploy.meaning: The rescue team used a helicopter to reach the stranded walkers.
deploy.clue: During the floods, the council used its small army of volunteers to carry food to cut-off villages.

deposit.meaning: We must remember the second half of the trip cost is due in June.
deposit.clue: I paid my club membership money into the bank this morning, so the coach is expecting me at training.

depot.meaning: The drivers collect parcels from there in the early morning before the shops open.
depot.clue: Boxes of spare parts are stacked there, waiting until a lorry comes to take them away.

depraved.meaning: He showed no guilt at all about the terrible things he had done to the family.
depraved.clue: The story tells how the evil official cheated poor families out of their savings for years on end.

deprecate.meaning: The head said she regretted the closing of the art club.
deprecate.clue: Local newspapers have long roundly criticised the council for wasting money on an empty car park.

depressing.meaning: The news about the factory closing made everyone in the town feel low.
depressing.clue: Grey clouds hung over the playing fields for a week, and the endless rain made everyone long for summer.

derail.meaning: The heavy rain put paid to our plans for the school picnic.
derail.clue: Late deliveries delayed the building work, so the new roof was not ready for the autumn term.

deranged.meaning: His behaviour yesterday was so strange that we were all worried about him.
deranged.clue: She began screaming at the television and pulling her hair, which worried everyone in the room.

deride.meaning: The class laughed at Sam's accent, which made him feel very unwelcome.
deride.clue: Rather than join the others in laughing, Priya spoke up and asked them to stop.

derision.meaning: His painting was met with sneers and laughter, and he never hung it up.
derision.clue: When she read her poem out, some boys sniggered, which filled the room with cruel amusement.

derisive.meaning: He answered my question with a laugh and a shrug, which annoyed me a lot.
derisive.clue: The crowd let out a jeer as the clumsy defender tripped over his own feet again.

derivative.meaning: Her essay was the same as everyone else's, with only the name on it changed.
derivative.clue: The painting seemed to the panel to copy an older master, so the young artist felt crushed.

description.meaning: Her account of the flat made the agent think it was much grander than it really was.
description.clue: The website lists every walking route in detail, including distances, hills and where to rest.

desecration.meaning: Local people were angry when litter and graffiti covered the war memorial.
desecration.clue: The vandals broke the old church windows, and the whole town was shocked by the damage.

desolate.meaning: The abandoned mining village stood in ruins, with weeds growing through the cracked roofs.
desolate.clue: We walked for hours across the empty moor, where not a single tree or farm could be seen.

despondent.meaning: He was in low spirits after the third rejection from the school.
despondent.clue: After weeks of losses, the captain sat in the empty changing room staring at his boots.

despot.meaning: The cruel ruler ignored the law and had his own enemies put in prison.
despot.clue: Anyone who disagreed with the king was imprisoned, and no one dared to speak freely.

desultory.meaning: He packed his bag slowly, putting one book in and then taking it out again.
desultory.clue: Their discussion drifted from football to music to lunch and never settled on anything useful.

detached.meaning: She kept her voice level and answered every question in a businesslike way.
detached.clue: During the discussion she stayed cool and answered questions in a calm, matter-of-fact way.

detain.meaning: The police held the two men at the station for questioning.
detain.clue: The officers kept the driver waiting at the roadside while they checked his papers.

determine.meaning: After weighing up the options, the head made up her mind and announced the result.
determine.clue: Years of practice were the thing which finally led the team to win the trophy.

deterrent.meaning: The possibility of being caught made the boys think twice before shoplifting.
deterrent.clue: CCTV cameras were fitted outside the shops to put off anyone planning to steal.

detractors.meaning: Despite all the criticism, the plan went ahead and the new building opened in April.
detractors.clue: Few people backed the new rule at first, but it seems to be working well now.

devious.meaning: He got the job by pretending to be friends with the boss rather than by ability.
devious.clue: The salesman was careful never to look at the price tag, in case he was asked about it.

devise.meaning: The engineers came up with a new way to save water in the swimming pool.
devise.clue: Our group thought of a clever way to record the results without any extra paper.

devote.meaning: She spends all her spare time helping at the local animal shelter.
devote.clue: After retiring, he gives every Tuesday to walking dogs for a local charity.

devour.meaning: The hungry boys finished the whole tray of sandwiches in a couple of minutes.
devour.clue: After the long walk, the hikers attacked their packed lunch beside the river.

dexterous.meaning: The surgeon performed the delicate operation with astonishing lightness of touch.
dexterous.clue: A potter's hands move so smoothly that the clay seems to rise on its own.

diabolical.meaning: His cruel plot would have trapped the children in the burning hall without anyone knowing.
diabolical.clue: The villain's plan was perfect in its cruelty, and the whole village trembled at the thought.

diagnose.meaning: The doctor examined her throat and decided she had a bad throat infection.
diagnose.clue: Our headmistress looked into the problem and found that the heating system had broken down.

diatribe.meaning: He launched into a long angry complaint that lasted for twenty minutes.
diatribe.clue: Rather than explain her plan, the manager simply attacked the committee's work in public.

diction.meaning: His sharp, formal way of speaking made the announcements sound rather grand.
diction.clue: Her clear, simple way with words meant even the youngest child could follow the story.

diffident.meaning: The new pupil was too nervous to ask the teacher for help.
diffident.clue: Too embarrassed to speak, she stood by the door and let others go first.

diffuse.meaning: The smell of the burning toast spread through the whole flat within seconds.
diffuse.clue: Sunlight poured through the window and filled every corner of the old kitchen.

digest.meaning: Eating too quickly means the body has far less time to take the goodness from food.
digest.clue: Fat and protein take much longer to break down in the body than fruit and vegetables do.

digression.meaning: The speaker lost track of the argument and started talking about his holiday.
digression.clue: We thought the talk was about science, but the teacher chatted about football for ages.

dim.meaning: Nobody could read the noticeboard until the caretaker replaced the dead bulb.
dim.clue: The path ahead was hard to see, so we walked slowly and used a torch.

diminution.meaning: A making smaller in size or amount, often over a period of time.
diminution.clue: The council faced a sharp diminution in funding, so several community projects had to be cancelled before the end of the year.

disappointed.meaning: Feeling sad because you had hoped for something better and it did not happen.
disappointed.clue: We were disappointed when the school trip was cancelled at the weekend, as we had already packed our sandwiches and coats.

disband.meaning: To make an organisation or team stop existing by telling everyone to leave.
disband.clue: The coach decided to disband the under-11 football team after only one season, saying that nobody had shown enough commitment.

discern.meaning: To see or understand something that is not easy to see or notice at first.
discern.clue: Even in the busy playground, Ms Patel could discern a worried expression on Amy's face and knew something was wrong.

discontent.meaning: A state of being dissatisfied or uneasy about the way things are.
discontent.clue: There has been growing discontent among parents about the long queues at the school gates every single morning.

discreet.meaning: Careful and quiet about something so that people do not notice it or feel upset.
discreet.clue: A discreet note from the head teacher explained the change to the playground arrangements without embarrassing anybody involved.

discrepancy.meaning: A gap between two accounts, figures or descriptions that ought to agree.
discrepancy.clue: The auditor found a discrepancy between the school's published budget and the actual amount of money in its account.

discretionary.meaning: Something you are allowed to do or have because a person decided to allow it, rather than because of a rule.
discretionary.clue: The grant covers travel costs, but the purchase of new computer games for the library is entirely discretionary this year.

discriminating.meaning: Having good judgement and the ability to tell fine differences between things.
discriminating.clue: Choosing a captain for the team needs a discriminating eye, because the coaches must weigh up many different qualities.

discursive.meaning: Moving from one topic to another without a clear main point.
discursive.clue: Mr Ali's discursive lecture wandered from Roman roads to his own holiday, so half the class stopped taking notes.

disdain.meaning: Showing that you think something is beneath you and is not worth serious attention.
disdain.clue: He glanced at the ancient cracked boots on display and viewed them with open disdain, muttering that they were rubbish.

dishearten.meaning: To make a person feel sad and less willing to keep trying.
dishearten.clue: Being left out of the team for three matches began to dishearten Joel, though his friends kept telling him to keep training.

disinclination.meaning: A feeling that you would rather not do something, with no strong reason given.
disinclination.clue: Her disinclination to join the drama club surprised nobody, since she has never once volunteered to perform on stage.

disintegrate.meaning: To fall to pieces gradually, either in a physical way or as an organisation.
disintegrate.clue: The old shed at the bottom of the garden began to disintegrate, so Dad insisted we kept well away from its door.

disinterested.meaning: Taking no side in a situation and judging it in a fair way.
disinterested.clue: Mr Hoyle, a disinterested judge, refused to say which finalist he preferred and simply scored each performance.

dismantle.meaning: To separate something that was built into its parts one by one.
dismantle.clue: In technology lessons we had to dismantle an old clock safely, lay every part on a tray, then label each one.

disparage.meaning: To put someone or something down by claiming it lacks worth or value.
disparage.clue: Rather than disparage the younger players' efforts, the coach highlighted their improvement and promised them more matches next season.

disparate.meaning: So different from each other that they have almost nothing in common.
disparate.clue: The teacher gathered a disparate collection of objects from the cupboard, including a bicycle bell and a plastic dinosaur.

disparity.meaning: A situation in which two people or groups are treated very differently because of their wealth or status.
disparity.clue: The report highlighted a wide disparity in exam results between pupils receiving free school meals and those whose families could pay for extra tuition.

dispassionate.meaning: Calm and controlled, especially when dealing with a difficult or unfair situation.
dispassionate.clue: Despite the furious complaints from the crowd, the linesman stayed dispassionate and explained his decision calmly to the referee.

dispel.meaning: To drive away a worry, doubt or unpleasant idea from a person's head.
dispel.clue: The head teacher's cheerful announcement helped dispel the rumours that our school would lose its playing fields to houses.

dispense.meaning: To give out something that is normally kept in store for later use.
dispense.clue: Volunteers at the fair dispense sweets and free programmes to visitors while the school band plays on the stage behind.

disputatious.meaning: Someone who loves arguing and will never admit that they are wrong.
disputatious.clue: Our new neighbour is so disputatious that he argued with the postman about a garden fence, then with the milkman about a bottle.

disseminate.meaning: To pass news, advice or instructions on to a large number of people.
disseminate.clue: Head teachers often disseminate the new uniform guidelines by email, on the noticeboard and in a letter to every family.

dissent.meaning: The act of expressing an opinion that differs from the one most people hold.
dissent.clue: Two governors recorded their dissent from the proposal, arguing that the new parking charges would harm local small businesses.

dissipate.meaning: To cause energy, liquid or a feeling to spread out and vanish.
dissipate.clue: Bright sunlight can dissipate the smell of burnt toast, so Mum opened every window in the kitchen.

dissonance.meaning: A combination of notes or opinions that sound or feel badly matched.
dissonance.clue: The music teacher asked the class why the two scales sounded so different, and then tapped out their dissonance on the piano.

dissuade.meaning: To talk somebody out of a plan or intention by giving them good reasons.
dissuade.clue: Ms Iqbal tried to dissuade Reece from skipping revision, showing him how many marks he had lost in past papers.

distant.meaning: Far away in distance, or a long way off in the past or the future.
distant.clue: On clear winter mornings you can see distant hills from our classroom window, and my grandfather remembers them well.

distasteful.meaning: Something you find unappealing and wish you had never tasted or seen.
distasteful.clue: The new cafe's strange smelling soup tasted distasteful to me, so I ate the crisps and drank the water instead.

distinct.meaning: Noticeably different from something else, so that the two can be told apart.
distinct.clue: There was a distinct difference between her two drawings, and the marker praised the way she had shaded the sky.

distinguished.meaning: Having earned great respect and honour from other people.
distinguished.clue: Our head teacher is a distinguished scientist, yet she still takes the time to talk to every class each morning.

distraction.meaning: Anything that makes you stop paying attention to what you are doing.
distraction.clue: With the television blaring in the next room, Tomas found it almost impossible to finish his history homework without a distraction.

disturbing.meaning: Making you feel worried because something strange or bad has happened.
disturbing.clue: A strange noise behind the shed was disturbing, so we hurried back into the house and rang Dad at work.

disused.meaning: Kept where it is but never used, like an old path that grass has covered.
disused.clue: Behind the gym stands a disused changing room, and the caretaker says it will become a quiet reading space next year.

divergent.meaning: Moving apart, so that people or things no longer agree or follow the same path.
divergent.clue: The two groups took divergent paths after the debate, one towards science club and the other towards the newspaper.

diverse.meaning: Made up of a wide range of different kinds, sizes or backgrounds.
diverse.clue: Our football club has a diverse squad, with players from fifteen different countries and just as many languages.

divine.meaning: Connected with a god or religion, or sometimes describing something wonderful.
divine.clue: The cathedral guide explained that the divine paintings on the ceiling told the story of the town since medieval times.

doctrine.meaning: A body of beliefs that a group or religion teaches and expects people to follow.
doctrine.clue: Our RE teacher explained the doctrine behind the school motto, which asks every pupil to be truthful and kind.

dogmatic.meaning: So sure of your own beliefs that you will not consider other ideas at all.
dogmatic.clue: His dogmatic refusal to share equipment caused an argument, and the referee finally made both teams shake hands.

dormant.meaning: Existing but doing nothing for a while, like a volcano that has not yet erupted.
dormant.clue: Volcanoes can stay dormant for thousands of years, so scientists keep checking the ground near this quiet hillside village.

dour.meaning: Having a serious, unfriendly expression with no sign of a smile.
dour.clue: Our dour headteacher looked thoroughly unimpressed by the joke, but the class laughed at it for a full minute.

doyen.meaning: The longest-serving and most respected person within a professional group.
doyen.clue: Our oldest inspector, known as the doyen of the group, applauded the invention that two Year 6 pupils had built.

drift.meaning: To be carried slowly across water or air, or to move aimlessly.
drift.clue: Autumn leaves drift across the playground after a strong wind, and the caretaker sweeps them into a heap.

droll.meaning: Strange and amusing, making people smile rather than laugh out loud.
droll.clue: His droll impression of the headteacher fooled us all, and the entire class burst into giggles at once.

dubious.meaning: Feeling that you cannot be sure about a fact, a person or whether something is real.
dubious.clue: We were dubious about the story one pupil told, since it seemed far too strange to be true.

dumb.meaning: Not able to speak, or staying so quiet that nobody can hear you.
dumb.clue: In the assembly the whole class went dumb with nerves, and only our headteacher managed to speak.

duplicity.meaning: Hiding your real plans behind a show of honesty, usually to gain something.
duplicity.clue: The letter revealed the manager's duplicity, claiming he knew nothing while secretly selling off the club's land.

durable.meaning: Made to last a long time and to survive rough everyday use.
durable.clue: Our new lockers are made of durable metal, so they should survive years of bags being thrown against them.

duration.meaning: How long an event, meeting or activity lasts from start to finish.
duration.clue: The duration of the revision course is six weeks, with two sessions each week after the final bell has rung.

duress.meaning: Being forced to do something you do not want to do because someone is threatening you.
duress.clue: The thief claimed the confession was made under duress, but nobody believed a word of it.

dutiful.meaning: Doing the right thing and carrying out your duties well, especially to a parent or an older person.
dutiful.clue: Such a dutiful son, he tidied the kitchen before breakfast and never argued about homework.

dynasty.meaning: A family that has handed down power or great wealth to its children for several generations.
dynasty.clue: Once a poor farming family, the Russells became a powerful dynasty of landowners over three generations.

earnest.meaning: Being completely serious about something, because you care about it a great deal.
earnest.clue: Her earnest plea for more time playing outside was ignored by the coach throughout the whole match.

ebullient.meaning: Being full of cheerful energy and excitement that seems to spill over all around you.
ebullient.clue: After the team's last-minute win, the ebullient captain ran around the pavilion shouting and hugging everyone.

echelon.meaning: One of the levels or steps in an organisation, from the most important people at the top to the least important.
echelon.clue: Only the top echelon of the school met the visiting inspectors, while the rest of us carried on with lessons.

eclectic.meaning: Deliberately mixing many different kinds of things together, such as music, furniture or ideas from several countries.
eclectic.clue: Her bedroom was eclectic, with Indian cotton curtains, a Japanese print and a battered English armchair.

eclipse.meaning: When one planet or star passes in front of another and hides it, or when something important suddenly loses the attention it used to get.
eclipse.clue: We sat in the garden with special glasses on, waiting for the eclipse to darken the afternoon sky.

edible.meaning: Something is edible when it is completely safe for you to eat.
edible.clue: The guide explained which wild berries were edible and which would make us ill if we ate them.

editor.meaning: The person whose job is to get a written work ready, correcting mistakes and checking every detail.
editor.clue: Before the story went to print, the editor removed two whole chapters and shortened the ending.

efface.meaning: To make marks disappear completely, so that there is no trace of them left.
efface.clue: Rain washed the chalk from the wall and almost effaced the message her brother had left there.

efficacious.meaning: Something that is efficacious is able to do exactly what it was designed to do.
efficacious.clue: The headmistress explained that the new reading scheme was efficacious, and the results proved her right.

effigy.meaning: A dummy or model made to look like a real person, sometimes displayed or burnt to show contempt.
effigy.clue: Crowds in the square cheered as a huge straw effigy of the tyrant was pulled down and set alight.

effusion.meaning: A sudden, uncontrolled flow of tears, emotion or liquid, often more than someone expected.
effusion.clue: Nobody expected such an effusion of tears when the announcement about the cancelled match was made.

egalitarian.meaning: Treating everyone as equals, so that no person or group is thought to be more important than another.
egalitarian.clue: Their egalitarian policy meant every pupil, even the youngest, had a vote in choosing the class play.

egotistical.meaning: Someone who is egotistical talks about their own achievements and thinks nobody else matters.
egotistical.clue: His egotistical habit of naming the school in every speech made the other pupils roll their eyes.

elated.meaning: So happy about something that you can hardly sit still or talk normally.
elated.clue: The team was elated when the winning goal went in during the last minute of the match.

elect.meaning: To make one person, rather than another, become the holder of an official post.
elect.clue: The pupils will elect a new captain on Friday, so every candidate is readying a short speech.

eloquent.meaning: Able to speak in a way that is fluent, confident and moves people to agree with you.
eloquent.clue: Her eloquent speech at the assembly persuaded the headteacher to keep the library open at lunchtimes.

elusive.meaning: Describing something that keeps slipping away from you, so you can never quite catch or understand it.
elusive.clue: The answer stayed elusive all morning, and by lunchtime the whole class had run out of ideas.

emanate.meaning: To come from a particular source and spread out into the surrounding air.
emanate.clue: A smell of fresh bread emanated from the bakery as soon as the school gate opened.

embargo.meaning: A rule put in place to stop something taking place, usually trade or the publishing of news.
embargo.clue: While the embargo was in force, journalists were not allowed to report the result of the vote.

embellish.meaning: To make a story or object sound or look grander by adding extra, often invented, details.
embellish.clue: His account of the holiday was heavily embellished, with three impossible rescues and a lost suitcase.

embody.meaning: To be the living example of a quality, or to contain a particular quality in yourself.
embody.clue: She embodies the spirit of the school, always helping quietly without ever seeking praise.

embrace.meaning: To take someone or something to your heart, with warmth and complete enthusiasm.
embrace.clue: The club embraced the new rule about phone use and changed its behaviour overnight.

embroil.meaning: To drag somebody into a dispute or difficulty that they cannot easily get out of.
embroil.clue: The rumour embroiled three families in a bitter argument that lasted for weeks.

eminent.meaning: Held in high respect by everybody in a particular field, because of what you have achieved.
eminent.clue: The eminent historian who visited our school had written fifteen books on the Roman army.

empathy.meaning: Understanding exactly how somebody else feels because you have felt that way yourself.
empathy.clue: His empathy was obvious when he noticed that the new girl was upset and left her alone.

emphasis.meaning: Deliberately drawing attention to one part of something because you want it noticed.
emphasis.clue: The headteacher put emphasis on reading aloud, so every lesson had a story time.

emphasise.meaning: To make people notice a particular point by giving it extra weight in what you say.
emphasise.clue: The coach chose to emphasise one lesson only: fair play mattered more than winning.

emphatic.meaning: Saying something in a strong, definite voice so that nobody is left in any doubt.
emphatic.clue: Her emphatic denial ended the argument, and the class accepted that she was telling the truth.

employ.meaning: To pay a person to do a job, or to put something such as a tool to work for you.
employ.clue: The school will employ four new helpers to run the busy lunch club this term.

emulate.meaning: To copy the way somebody does something because you think they do it better than you.
emulate.clue: Our class tried to emulate the older pupils and started running the library in the same way.

enamour.meaning: To fall deeply in love with something, or to be so charmed by it that you cannot help liking it.
enamour.clue: The whole class was enamoured of the new caretaker, who organised a treasure hunt for them.

endorse.meaning: To put your name behind someone because you believe they are good.
endorse.clue: Several well-known players endorsed the school's appeal by donating signed shirts for the auction.

engender.meaning: To cause a strong feeling or a lasting situation to develop among people.
engender.clue: The decision to extend homework engendered fierce argument between pupils, parents and even the headteacher.

engrossed.meaning: Giving every thought and all your energy to one activity, so you miss everything around you.
engrossed.clue: She was engrossed in her book and did not hear the bell ring at the end of the day.

enigmatic.meaning: Describing something that puzzles you because nobody seems to know the answer.
enigmatic.clue: The enigmatic noise coming from the empty hall became a favourite subject of guesswork.

enormous.meaning: So large that it is impossible to take in at one look, or so big in amount that it seems endless.
enormous.clue: The amount of homework set over the holidays was enormous and kept three classes in for days.

enthralling.meaning: Holding your attention so completely that you forget about everything else happening around you.
enthralling.clue: The museum's display of ancient armour was so enthralling that we stayed an hour past the bell.

enthusiast.meaning: Someone who loves a subject so much that they want to talk about it or do it all the time.
enthusiast.clue: Every football enthusiast in the year group turned out to support the school's new team.

entice.meaning: To persuade somebody to do something they might not otherwise do, by making it sound appealing.
entice.clue: A voucher enticed many parents to visit the book fair on Saturday morning.

entreat.meaning: To ask someone for something in a way that shows how much you need it.
entreat.clue: The head boy entreated the governors to keep the pool open over the winter.

enumerate.meaning: To set out every single item separately, one after another, in a fixed order.
enumerate.clue: She had to enumerate every item in the lost property box before she could leave.

envisage.meaning: To picture how something might turn out before it actually happens.
envisage.clue: She could not envisage winning the race, yet she trained hard every single evening.

ephemeral.meaning: Something that disappears very quickly, lasting only minutes, days or weeks rather than years.
ephemeral.clue: The rainbow over the sports field was ephemeral, vanishing within a minute of appearing.

epic.meaning: A story, achievement or plan that is impressively large, brave and larger than life.
epic.clue: Their epic attempt to build a raft from old planks ended in triumph at the swimming pool.

epiphany.meaning: The moment when the answer suddenly becomes obvious to you after puzzling over it for a long time.
epiphany.clue: Her epiphany came on the bus, when she suddenly saw why the numbers would not add up.

episodic.meaning: Unfolding in short separate instalments rather than in one smooth, flowing narrative.
episodic.clue: His episodic diary recorded only the exciting days, leaving the long quiet weeks blank.

epoch.meaning: A whole stretch of history, defined by one big change such as a new invention or a different ruler.
epoch.clue: The invention of the printing press marks an epoch in the way people shared knowledge.

equanimity.meaning: The quiet steadiness that lets somebody keep calm when things go wrong.
equanimity.clue: Despite the noise and the clock running out, she finished her speech with remarkable equanimity.

equivocal.meaning: An answer that avoids committing to anything, so nobody can be sure what it really means.
equivocal.clue: When the coach asked why she had missed the match, her equivocal reply left everyone in the class guessing.

era.meaning: A stretch of years that historians group together because of the things happening in it.
era.clue: Our teacher said the Industrial Revolution was an era of invention, but it also brought terrible conditions for many workers.

erasable.meaning: Something that can be taken back or rubbed out, so it does not stay for ever.
erasable.clue: The whiteboard marker left a faint mark, and the teacher said the ink was erasable with a dry cloth.

erect.meaning: Someone who is erect holds their body perfectly upright, as if standing to attention.
erect.clue: He sat erect in the assembly hall, hands on his knees, waiting for the headteacher to walk past.

erratic.meaning: Something that keeps changing in a way nobody can predict or rely on.
erratic.clue: His erratic handwriting made the teacher's marking slow, since the letters jumped about the page.

erroneous.meaning: An idea, figure or report that is simply wrong because somebody got it wrong.
erroneous.clue: The newspaper printed an erroneous story about the local school before running a correction the next day.

erudite.meaning: A person who knows a surprising amount about history, literature or science.
erudite.clue: Our guest, an erudite professor, explained why Roman roads were still standing after two thousand years.

esoteric.meaning: Ideas so specialised and strange that people outside that field cannot make sense of them.
esoteric.clue: The article discussed an esoteric mathematical proof that only a handful of readers in the world could follow.

espouse.meaning: To say in public that you believe in something and will argue for it.
espouse.clue: Several parents came to the meeting to espouse the idea of a pedestrian crossing outside the school gates.

essence.meaning: The heart of something, the small part that really matters once everything else is stripped away.
essence.clue: The speaker said the essence of good writing is saying one thing clearly in as few words as possible.

esteem.meaning: A feeling of genuine regard that we hold for somebody and show in how we treat them.
esteem.clue: Years after leaving school, she still holds the old caretaker in high esteem for her kindness.

estimate.meaning: To form a rough idea of how much something costs or how many there are, without exact proof.
estimate.clue: Estimate the number of words on this page before we start reading, then we will compare your guess.

ethereal.meaning: Something so light and delicate that it seems more like a dream than a real thing.
ethereal.clue: A thin ethereal mist drifted over the pond while the first early birds began to sing.

eulogy.meaning: Kind words spoken about somebody, usually said aloud just after they have died.
eulogy.clue: At the funeral, his cousin gave a eulogy that made the whole family laugh and cry at once.

euphemism.meaning: A way of describing something that sounds gentler and more polite than the real word.
euphemism.clue: Saying that somebody has passed away is a euphemism, chosen because it sounds kinder than saying they have died.

euphonious.meaning: A voice or noise that is smooth and musical rather than rough and unpleasant to listen to.
euphonious.clue: The choir director praised the euphonious sound the children made together after only three rehearsals.

euphoria.meaning: A short burst of wonderful happiness that makes a person feel as if they might burst.
euphoria.clue: There was pure euphoria in the hall when the last goal arrived, and everybody jumped onto the benches.

evacuate.meaning: To move everyone out of a place quickly because a flood, fire or bomb makes it unsafe.
evacuate.clue: The school had to evacuate the hall when a pipe burst and water poured across the floor.

evanescent.meaning: Something so short-lived that you look again and it has already gone.
evanescent.clue: The rainbow above the football pitch was evanescent, and in less than a minute the rain had washed it away.

evolve.meaning: To change slowly and steadily, developing into a more advanced or different form.
evolve.clue: The syllabus explains how species evolve, since birds and dinosaurs share a common ancestor millions of years ago.

exacerbate.meaning: To pile further difficulties onto something that was already going badly.
exacerbate.clue: The heavy rain exacerbated the flooding, and the council brought thousands of sandbags to the riverbank.

exacting.meaning: A task or person that will not settle for anything less than perfect work.
exacting.clue: The exacting coach made the choir rehearse the same difficult passage for forty minutes.

exalt.meaning: To lift somebody up in the eyes of others by speaking of them in glowing terms.
exalt.clue: The old local poet was exalted by the council, which named the community library after her.

exciting.meaning: Something that makes you want to watch it or take part straight away.
exciting.clue: The final of the cup was so exciting that our normally quiet class shouted with every shot on goal.

exemplary.meaning: Behaviour so good that a teacher might point to it as an example for everybody else.
exemplary.clue: Her exemplary conduct in the library, sitting quietly while others chatted, earned her a gold badge.

exemplify.meaning: To prove a general point by pointing to a particular case that shows it clearly.
exemplify.clue: The teacher used the broken window to exemplify why our class must look after the playground equipment.

exempt.meaning: Officially allowed to ignore a rule or to avoid paying something.
exempt.clue: Pupils who are exempt from the charge for music lessons may use the practice room instead.

exhaustive.meaning: A study or search that has checked absolutely everything, leaving nothing untested.
exhaustive.clue: After an exhaustive search of the changing rooms, the PE teacher found the missing kit under a bench.

exhilarating.meaning: Something so enjoyable that it leaves you feeling full of energy and ready for more.
exhilarating.clue: The ride down the steep blue slide was so exhilarating that they begged for another turn.

exhort.meaning: To speak firmly to somebody, pushing them to act rather than merely suggesting it.
exhort.clue: The captain exhorted the team to keep their heads up after that disastrous first half.

exonerate.meaning: To state officially that somebody who was suspected has in fact done nothing wrong.
exonerate.clue: New evidence exonerated the caretaker, and the headteacher apologised to her in front of the governors.

expanse.meaning: A great wide-open space you can hardly see across, like an empty beach or plain sky.
expanse.clue: From the top of the hill we looked out across an expanse of fields that went on for miles and miles.

expedient.meaning: A quick, useful way of dealing with a problem, even though it feels a little too easy.
expedient.clue: Painting the fence looked like an expedient, but the headteacher rightly demanded proper repairs.

expedite.meaning: To hurry a job along so that it is finished sooner than anybody expected.
expedite.clue: Sending the forms by email helped to expedite the decision, and results arrived within a week.

expel.meaning: To make somebody leave a place they belong to, by an official order.
expel.clue: The referee had to expel two players from the pitch after the fight, and both teams left disappointed.

expense.meaning: The money a thing costs, or the money that a job or trip takes out of the budget.
expense.clue: The school trip came to a total expense of eighteen pounds per pupil this year.

expert.meaning: A person who really knows their subject and can be trusted to give good advice.
expert.clue: For our history project we interviewed an expert on the Roman army about training and marching routes.

explicit.meaning: Instructions given in plain words, so that nobody can be unsure what they mean.
explicit.clue: The directions for the experiment were explicit, so nobody could be surprised by the results.

expository.meaning: Non-fiction writing that sets out facts and explains them, as in a textbook or an information leaflet.
expository.clue: The library books about the Romans include expository chapters explaining how roads and aqueducts were built.

expunge.meaning: To rub something out for good, taking it from a record so that it no longer counts.
expunge.clue: The examiner instructed the school to expunge the invalid paper from the results table altogether.

exquisite.meaning: Something so finely and beautifully made that every tiny detail is a treat to look at.
exquisite.clue: The jeweller showed us an exquisite silver watch, its case covered in tiny flowers cut by hand.

extended.meaning: Going on for much longer than usual, or stretched out to a greater length.
extended.clue: The extended rain spell kept our sports day inside the hall for the third day running.

extol.meaning: To describe something in glowing words because you think it is wonderful.
extol.clue: The headteacher loved to extol the pupils who had tidied the corridor without being asked.

extract.meaning: To take a piece out of a bigger whole, such as a passage out of a book.
extract.clue: From her diary she chose one moving extract to read aloud to the class in assembly.

extraneous.meaning: Extra material that has nothing to do with the point and can safely be cut out.
extraneous.clue: The editor cut several extraneous paragraphs, keeping only the parts that answered the question.

extraordinary.meaning: Something so unusual that it makes people stop and stare, or ask how on earth it happened.
extraordinary.clue: The village had an extraordinary summer, with sunflowers taller than the children in the playing field.

extricate.meaning: To get a person or animal out of a situation they cannot get out of by themselves.
extricate.clue: It took the fire crew an hour to extricate two drivers from the overturned van on the motorway.

extrovert.meaning: Somebody who enjoys company, talks easily to strangers and is never embarrassed to speak up.
extrovert.clue: As a real extrovert, she volunteered to introduce herself to every family at the school open evening.

exuberance.meaning: A great rush of lively energy and excitement about whatever is happening.
exuberance.clue: The toddlers greeted the clowns with such exuberance that one of them dropped his balloon.

fabricate.meaning: Fabricating a message means making something up so that it passes as genuine when it is not.
fabricate.clue: The careless boy admitted that he had fabricated an email to pretend he had done his homework.

facade.meaning: The front of an old town hall can look like a palace while the rooms inside are shabby and damp.
facade.clue: The impressive facade of the museum fooled us, as the galleries inside were tiny and dusty.

fact.meaning: A fact can be checked and shown to be true, whereas an opinion is simply what somebody thinks.
fact.clue: Our teacher asked for proof before accepting any claim, reminding us that a fact must always be supported by evidence.

faint.meaning: A faint noise is so quiet that you must strain to hear it, and a faint mark is almost invisible.
faint.clue: There was a faint smell of smoke in the corridor, but the fire alarm did not go off.

fallacious.meaning: A fallacious argument reaches the wrong conclusion through a hidden flaw, however persuasive it may sound.
fallacious.clue: The pupil's conclusion was fallacious, because he assumed that every visitor came by train.

falter.meaning: To falter is to lose your confidence or your balance before you have finished what you started.
falter.clue: The old ladder faltered as he stepped onto the top rung, and he had to stop and breathe.

fanaticism.meaning: Fanaticism goes far beyond genuine enthusiasm, refusing to listen to any view that differs.
fanaticism.clue: His fanaticism about his team turned every friendly match into an argument he had to win.

farce.meaning: A farce is a ridiculous comedy in which everybody behaves in silly, exaggerated ways.
farce.clue: The play was such a farce that we laughed at every entrance and hardly listened to a word.

fastidious.meaning: Being fastidious means noticing every speck of dust and never settling for anything less than perfect.
fastidious.clue: Our fastidious head teacher checks every line of the display board before the parents arrive.

fateful.meaning: A fateful choice is one that changes everything that happens afterwards, for better or worse.
fateful.clue: The coach blamed his fateful decision to drop the strongest runner just before the race.

fathom.meaning: Nobody could understand why the new pupil never spoke to anybody in the dining hall.
fathom.clue: Even the head teacher could not fathom how the password for the site had been changed.

fatuous.meaning: A fatuous remark has no point at all, rather like saying that opening a window will close a door.
fatuous.clue: His fatuous idea of wearing a hat to the swimming lesson made the whole class burst out laughing.

feasible.meaning: Building a new library within a year is feasible if the council has enough money and workers.
feasible.clue: Finishing the model castle by Friday is feasible, provided that we start today.

feckless.meaning: A feckless team captain forgets the kit, misses the register and leaves the work undone.
feckless.clue: Our feckless goalkeeper let in three goals and then blamed the wet grass.

femininity.meaning: Studying femininity means asking why certain jobs and hobbies are thought to be only for girls.
femininity.clue: Our debate about femininity in the English lesson turned into a fierce argument about who plays football.

feral.meaning: A feral cat is one left to live outside with nobody looking after it, so it behaves like a wild animal.
feral.clue: Feral pigeons have taken over the car park and now dive at anyone holding a chip.

ferocity.meaning: The ferocity of the storm frightened the horses, which bolted as the first hail began to fall.
ferocity.clue: The dog defended its home with such ferocity that the postman refused to come again.

fervour.meaning: Fervour makes a supporter shout and wave his scarf whatever the score, win or lose.
fervour.clue: She sang the school anthem with such fervour that even the visiting parents began to clap.

festivity.meaning: The village held a summer party as its final festivity of the year, with music, bunting and cakes.
festivity.clue: The end-of-term festivity lasted three hours, and nobody went home until the rain started.

fiasco.meaning: A fiasco turns out far worse than anybody expected, and usually ends in total chaos.
fiasco.clue: Our school play was a fiasco, since nobody could remember their lines on the night.

finesse.meaning: Finesse means handling something delicate with light fingers rather than heavy-handed methods.
finesse.clue: He cracked the hard-boiled egg with such finesse that not a drop of yolk fell.

flagrant.meaning: A flagrant foul is one the referee can see clearly, such as pushing another player in the face.
flagrant.clue: Cheating in the exam was so flagrant that the invigilator stopped the whole paper immediately.

flattering.meaning: A flattering remark sounds lovely but leaves out the truth, so take it with a pinch of salt.
flattering.clue: His flattering comment about her singing did not make up for the way he spoke to her.

flawed.meaning: A flawed plan has a weakness somewhere that will cause trouble later on, even if it looks sound.
flawed.clue: The explanation had a flawed argument, so we asked the teacher to go over it again.

flawless.meaning: A flawless piece of work has no faults at all, so there is nothing to correct or improve.
flawless.clue: The picture he drew of the church was flawless, with every brick carefully outlined.

flee.meaning: To run away from danger is to head off at speed and not look back until you feel safe.
flee.clue: The frightened boys fled the baying dog and did not stop until they reached the gate.

flimsy.meaning: A flimsy cardboard box cannot hold the shopping when the wind blows hard against it.
flimsy.clue: The flimsy fence blew flat in the first gale, leaving the dog loose in the lane.

flippant.meaning: Making a flippant joke about somebody's grief is unkind, however much it makes people smile.
flippant.clue: His flippant answer about the funeral made his grandmother turn away in tears.

flora.meaning: In a rainforest the plant life is so dense that the narrow path is easy to lose.
flora.clue: The guide showed us the local flora, including a fern that is over two metres tall.

florid.meaning: Florid writing piles on fancy words until the plain meaning underneath is hidden.
florid.clue: We cut down the florid description and replaced it with two short clear sentences.

flout.meaning: Anyone who openly breaks the school uniform rule will be asked to see the head teacher.
flout.clue: Anyone who flouts the school uniform rule will be sent straight to see the head teacher.

foal.meaning: A newborn foal is born with long legs and can run within an hour of arriving in the world.
foal.clue: A foal can stand and run within an hour of being born, which astonished us.

foolhardy.meaning: It was foolhardy to swim out so far when the lifeguard had already given a warning.
foolhardy.clue: It was foolhardy of him to climb the old wall in the rain and jump down.

forbid.meaning: A school can forbid certain activities to keep everyone safe, and the rule applies to everybody.
forbid.clue: The rules forbid eating in the lab, so the pupils left their sandwiches outside.

forecast.meaning: A forecast is only a good guess about the future, and the weather changes its mind often.
forecast.clue: The forecast promised dry weather, so we put all the stools outside for the reading lesson.

foremost.meaning: The leading painter in Britain means the one who is known above every other artist.
foremost.clue: She is the foremost expert on the history of this village and has written two books.

foreshadow.meaning: Dark clouds on the horizon hint that a storm is coming, though they do not prove one will arrive.
foreshadow.clue: The empty stage foreshadowed disaster, because nobody had arrived with the scenery.

foresight.meaning: Foresight means reading the signs carefully so that you are ready for what is coming next.
foresight.clue: By packing a warm coat she showed great foresight, since the afternoon turned freezing.

forestall.meaning: Checking the food stores early stops the problem of running out over the weekend.
forestall.clue: Booking the tickets early forestalled the rush, so we still managed to travel together.

forge.meaning: Working with hot iron means heating it first so that it softens enough to be hammered into place.
forge.clue: A blacksmith's job is to forge horseshoes from hot iron using a hammer and anvil.

formidable.meaning: A team that has never lost is intimidating, because pupils expect to be beaten before they start.
formidable.clue: The exam looked formidable until I worked through a few questions and felt calmer.

forsake.meaning: To give up on a person or a task completely means refusing to help it any more.
forsake.clue: Fearing a storm at sea, the captain refused to forsake the small fishing boat.

forthcoming.meaning: The exam we all sit in June is the one everybody has been revising for since September.
forthcoming.clue: The forthcoming match has been moved to the new floodlit pitch behind the gym.

forthright.meaning: A direct answer gives you the truth straight away, even when it is not what you hoped to hear.
forthright.clue: Our forthright head teacher explained at once why the trip had been cancelled.

fortuitous.meaning: A welcome discovery made by chance is something nobody was looking for, and it could not have been arranged.
fortuitous.clue: By some fortuitous chance, the class found itself alone in the sports hall for an extra hour.

foster.meaning: Good teachers build up confidence by letting pupils try new things and fail safely.
foster.clue: The play fosters an interest in history by using real letters from the archive.

foundation.meaning: The base of a building has to carry the whole weight above it, so it must never crack.
foundation.clue: The reading room is built on a foundation of stone slabs from Victorian times.

fragment.meaning: When only a small part of an old manuscript survives, scholars can still learn a surprising amount from it.
fragment.clue: He dropped the mug and swept up every fragment before the teacher noticed.

frail.meaning: An elderly person can be very weak yet still be perfectly happy with the right care and company.
frail.clue: My great-aunt is frail now, so we carry the shopping up to her flat.

frantic.meaning: When people are desperate and late, they hurry so much that small mistakes are easily made.
frantic.clue: With the bus due in five minutes we were frantic, waving and shouting at the driver.

fraudulent.meaning: A fraudulent claim is a lie told on purpose so that somebody will pay money.
fraudulent.clue: The shopkeeper was caught selling fake designer labels, and the police called the whole thing criminal.

frequent.meaning: Something that is frequent happens a lot, rather than only now and then.
frequent.clue: The library runs a storytelling session every Friday, and the children look forward to it all week.

frightful.meaning: A frightful experience is so unpleasant that it upsets you just to think about it.
frightful.clue: The thunderstorm last night was so noisy that the little dog refused to come out from under the bed.

fulfilled.meaning: To feel fulfilled is to feel that you have achieved something you truly wanted to do.
fulfilled.clue: After months of rehearsals, the choir felt happy that all their hard work had finally paid off.

fund.meaning: A fund is money that has been saved or collected to pay for a particular job.
fund.clue: The school fund paid for more library books, so every class has plenty to read this term.

furnish.meaning: To furnish a room means to give it everything needed to make it comfortable to use.
furnish.clue: We helped carry desks and armchairs into the classroom and fill every shelf with books.

furtive.meaning: Someone who is furtive is trying not to be seen while they do something.
furtive.clue: The boy slipped the note across the desk, making sure that nobody else could see him do it.

gallant.meaning: A gallant person is brave and polite, and will not walk away from someone who needs help.
gallant.clue: The oldest boy in the class kept his head while the fire alarm rang, helping the younger children to the door.

galvanise.meaning: Something that galvanises people makes them suddenly full of energy and keen to act.
galvanise.clue: Winning the final last spring galvanised the school team, and they trained hard all summer.

garbled.meaning: When a message is garbled, the words have been jumbled together and it makes no sense.
garbled.clue: Several lines had been smudged so badly that the message made no sense to anyone who read it.

garment.meaning: A garment is one thing you wear, rather than all your clothes put together.
garment.clue: The shop had a rail of winter coats, and Mum found one that was not too expensive.

garrulous.meaning: A garrulous person finds it very hard to stop talking, even about nothing at all.
garrulous.clue: Our neighbour is such a chatterbox that a short walk to the shops takes a whole hour.

gauge.meaning: To gauge something is to form a judgement about it without weighing or measuring it.
gauge.clue: We could not work out how busy the park would be, so we set off early and found it crammed.

genealogy.meaning: Genealogy is the study of who your ancestors were, going back many generations.
genealogy.clue: Our class drew charts of where everyone came from and discovered that two pupils were distant cousins.

genre.meaning: A genre is a group of works that share the same kind of style, like all detective stories.
genre.clue: The bookshop has a whole shelf of detective novels, and she borrowed her first one on Friday.

genteel.meaning: To be genteel is to behave in a stiff, formal, old-fashioned way that seems oddly polite.
genteel.clue: He ordered the tea and spoke so formally that everyone at the table burst out laughing.
