gentility.meaning: Gentility means showing good manners and being careful never to upset anyone.
gentility.clue: The head teacher praised the class for the way they welcomed the visiting parents and gave up their seats.

glimpse.meaning: A glimpse is a very quick look that shows you only a moment of something before it goes.
glimpse.clue: Through the kitchen window we saw the fox for a second before it jumped over the fence and vanished.

glutton.meaning: A glutton is someone who always eats too much and never seems to be full.
glutton.clue: At the party Marcus ate three sandwiches, two muffins and a whole packet of crisps.

gluttonous.meaning: Gluttonous eating means stuffing yourself greedily, wanting more and more food.
gluttonous.clue: He filled his plate twice and then went back for a third helping of pudding.

goaded.meaning: If someone goads you into doing something, they keep needling you until you do it.
goaded.clue: He only agreed to join the team after his friends teased him about it for a week.

gorge.meaning: To gorge yourself on food means to eat as much of it as you can possibly manage.
gorge.clue: At the fair we both ate far too much pizza and could hardly move afterwards.

gracious.meaning: Someone gracious is politely and warmly kind, even to somebody who has hurt them.
gracious.clue: She was gracious about losing the match, congratulating the other team and offering them a drink.

grandeur.meaning: Grandeur is the sense of great, impressive beauty that something powerful and old gives you.
grandeur.clue: The old cathedral, with its painted ceiling and towering columns, takes your breath away.

grandiose.meaning: A grandiose claim sounds magnificent but is really more showy than it is real.
grandiose.clue: His claim to have built the greatest model railway in the country sounded far too large for one small bedroom.

granular.meaning: A granular substance is made of separate tiny pieces, so it feels rough between your fingers.
granular.clue: The sand in the toy tray was made of tiny separate pieces that you could feel between your fingers.

grate.meaning: If something grates on you, it keeps annoying you and you cannot relax.
grate.clue: The dripping tap wore on everyone all morning until Dad finally turned it off and fixed the leak.

gratuitous.meaning: A gratuitous act is one that serves no real purpose and did not need to happen at all.
gratuitous.clue: The film included a scene of violence that had nothing at all to do with the story.

gravity.meaning: Gravity is the serious, solemn manner that makes people behave quietly when something important happens.
gravity.clue: The headteacher made her announcement in such a solemn tone that nobody in the hall said a word.

grievance.meaning: A grievance is a complaint about something that was unfair, made by someone who feels badly treated.
grievance.clue: Several parents raised the issue with the office, saying they had not been told what the trip would cost.

gripe.meaning: Someone who gripes keeps making the same complaint, usually about something small and unimportant.
gripe.clue: He keeps making a fuss about the cold classroom, even on the warmest day of the year.

grotto.meaning: A grotto is a little rocky cave that you can walk into from the shore.
grotto.clue: At low tide we crawled through a low opening in the rocks and found crabs scuttling in the darkness.

grudge.meaning: To hold a grudge means keeping your anger about something that happened long ago.
grudge.clue: He never spoke to his brother again after the argument at Christmas, and he has not forgiven him to this day.

gruelling.meaning: A gruelling task is so tiring that you can hardly move when it is over.
gruelling.clue: Running the whole length of the park in the rain left us all desperate for a hot drink.

guard.meaning: To guard something means to watch over it so that nothing can harm it.
guard.clue: Two lollipop ladies guard the crossing so that we can get to school safely.

guffaw.meaning: A guffaw is a big, sudden laugh that shakes you and is far too loud for normal talking.
guffaw.clue: At the end of the show the whole audience burst out laughing at the final joke.

guile.meaning: Guile is the word for being sly and crafty and hiding what you really mean to do.
guile.clue: By promising a free holiday that did not exist, the salesman tricked my dad into paying a fortune.

guttural.meaning: A guttural sound comes from deep in the throat rather than from the mouth.
guttural.clue: The singer had such a deep voice that we could hardly make out the words on the slow song.

habitable.meaning: A habitable place is one where people could really live, with shelter, water and food.
habitable.clue: The island looked beautiful in the brochure, but with no water and nowhere to sleep, nobody could live there.

habitat.meaning: The habitat of a wild animal is the place where it is naturally found, not where it is kept.
habitat.clue: The peregrine falcon lives on remote sea cliffs, far from anywhere most people will ever visit.

habitually.meaning: Someone who acts habitually does the same thing again and again without thinking about it.
habitually.clue: Our neighbour never bothers to close the gate, so we check the latch every single time.

hackneyed.meaning: A hackneyed phrase is one everybody has heard so often that it no longer has any effect.
hackneyed.clue: The essay began with the usual tired phrase about the early bird catching the worm.

hallowed.meaning: A hallowed place has been respected for so long that people treat it as almost holy.
hallowed.clue: The old college chapel is used for services each Sunday, and visitors lower their voices inside.

halt.meaning: If something halts, it stops completely for a while and may then start again.
halt.clue: The queue of cars on the bridge did not move at all for ten minutes while a lorry crossed ahead.

haphazard.meaning: A haphazard attempt is untidy and unplanned, with no real order or system in it.
haphazard.clue: Our display looked a jumble because the two groups put up their posters without talking to each other.

hardy.meaning: A hardy plant can stand bitter wind and frost without dying back.
hardy.clue: The gardener picked a variety of shrub that can stand the cold, because this garden faces straight out to sea.

harmonious.meaning: Harmonious means that all the parts fit together well, with no fighting or clash between them.
harmonious.clue: The two brass sections fitted together so well that the whole band sounded like one instrument.

harrowing.meaning: A harrowing experience is deeply upsetting and stays in your memory long afterwards.
harrowing.clue: The film told a true story about a young couple who had lost everything in the flood.

haste.meaning: Haste means hurrying so much that you skip bits and make mistakes.
haste.clue: With the exam only a week away, she crammed in five chapters every evening and hardly slept.

havoc.meaning: To make havoc of something is to damage it and turn it into a total mess.
havoc.clue: When the storm tore the roof off the sports hall, every Saturday match had to be rearranged.

hearth.meaning: The warm part of a home where the family gathers to keep warm, which is why the word also stands for home.
hearth.clue: In that old cottage the hearth was the heart of everything, and the whole household gathered there each winter evening.

heartless.meaning: Someone who feels nothing for the pain of others and treats their suffering as unimportant.
heartless.clue: The landlord was heartless, throwing the family out onto the street in the middle of winter without a single thought for them.

hedonist.meaning: Someone who thinks having a good time and being comfortable matters more than duty, work or other people.
hedonist.clue: As a hedonist he spent every Saturday in the cafe, leaving the washing unwashed and the garden entirely to his neighbour.

heeding.meaning: Taking notice of what somebody has warned or asked you to do, and then doing it.
heeding.clue: By heeding the teacher's advice about revision, Priya managed to improve her maths grade by two full marks.

heedless.meaning: Not paying attention to a risk or a warning, and acting in a way that could easily lead to harm.
heedless.clue: It was heedless of his own safety to leave the bicycle unlocked in the playground, and by break it had vanished.

heresy.meaning: A belief that other people think is wrong because it challenges everything they have always been taught.
heresy.clue: In those days, suggesting that the Earth was round was treated as a serious heresy by many educated people.

heroic.meaning: Brave and admirable in a way that makes somebody seem like a hero.
heroic.clue: Her heroic effort to pull the little boy from the river impressed everyone watching from the bank.

hiatus.meaning: A stretch of time when something stops happening before it starts up again.
hiatus.clue: After a long hiatus during the summer holidays, the swimming club began training for the new season again.

hierarchy.meaning: A way of organising a group so that some people or things always come above the others.
hierarchy.clue: At our school the hierarchy was obvious: the head teacher made the rules and everyone else followed them.

hilarious.meaning: So amusing that you cannot help laughing out loud at it.
hilarious.clue: The pantomime was absolutely hilarious, and the whole audience was still chuckling long after the curtain fell.

hinge.meaning: A piece of metal that lets a door swing, and by extension the point at which something can change.
hinge.clue: The gate would not open at all, so Tom levered the rusty hinge loose with a screwdriver.

hoard.meaning: Someone who hides away supplies and never uses them, perhaps because they expect a shortage.
hoard.clue: My sister loves to hoard biscuits in her bedroom, and there is now an entire box hidden behind her wardrobe.

homogeneous.meaning: All of exactly the same sort, with no differences at all between the parts.
homogeneous.clue: The class was a homogeneous group, since every pupil had arrived the previous September from the same feeder school.

homograph.meaning: One of a pair of words that are written in exactly the same way but mean quite different things.
homograph.clue: Bat puzzled the pupils, since one written form covers two words with opposite meanings, and nobody could see why.

homophone.meaning: One of two words that are said in the same way but are written and understood differently.
homophone.clue: Their names are homophones, so the teacher wrote them both on the board to make sure nobody mixed them up.

hone.meaning: To make an ability better and sharper through hours of steady practice.
hone.clue: She spent every spare minute honing her tennis serve until her coach said the timing had improved enormously.

hoof.meaning: The hard, hollow part at the bottom of a horse's or cow's foot, which it stands and runs on.
hoof.clue: The pony stamped her hoof angrily on the wooden floor while we waited outside the stable.

horrendous.meaning: Extremely unpleasant and shocking, often making people very frightened or upset.
horrendous.clue: We had to cancel the trip because of the horrendous weather, which lashed the playground with wind and rain.

hospitable.meaning: Glad to have visitors and taking care to see that they feel at ease in your own home.
hospitable.clue: Our new neighbours were hospitable, knocking on our door with a warm cake the first afternoon they arrived.

hostility.meaning: A state of bitter anger between people or groups, in which each side treats the other badly.
hostility.clue: The crowd's hostility towards the visiting team was clear from the first whistle, and stewards stepped in early.

hubris.meaning: Acting as though you are better or stronger than everyone else, without knowing your real limits.
hubris.clue: The captain's hubris after winning the trophy led him to make comments that upset everybody in the club.

hue.meaning: A particular kind of colour, especially the way one shade blends into the next.
hue.clue: The artist mixed the paint carefully until she found just the right greenish hue for the distant hills.

humane.meaning: Treating people and animals with kindness and pity instead of causing them harm.
humane.clue: He was praised for his humane treatment of the injured badger, which he nursed back to health.

humble.meaning: Quiet and modest about yourself, without showing off what you are good at.
humble.clue: Despite his humble manner, Oliver had solved the hardest maths problem in the whole of Year Six.

humorous.meaning: Showing a sense of fun that makes other people smile and laugh.
humorous.clue: Her humorous speech at the assembly had everyone roaring, and even the head teacher could not keep a straight face.

hybrid.meaning: A thing that combines two quite different kinds, such as an animal bred from two others.
hybrid.clue: The garden centre sold a hybrid that combined a plum and a peach, so its fruit tasted like both.

hyperbole.meaning: Saying that something is far bigger or worse than it really is, simply for effect.
hyperbole.clue: His claim about waiting a whole year for the bus was pure hyperbole, since the delay was minutes.

hypocritical.meaning: Saying that you care about doing the right thing but then behaving badly in private.
hypocritical.clue: It seemed hypocritical when the head praised truthfulness while quietly hiding a mistake she had herself made.

hypothetical.meaning: Concerning something that is only imagined, which may well happen but has not happened yet.
hypothetical.clue: The debate team practised answering hypothetical questions, such as what they would do if they won.

idiom.meaning: A saying where the words taken separately do not mean what the whole phrase really means.
idiom.clue: He told the class that missing the bus was a piece of bad luck, and they laughed at the saying.

idle.meaning: Not working and having nothing to do, either by choice or because there is nothing to do.
idle.clue: On the last afternoon of term the staff room was idle, and even the caretaker sat in the sunshine.

idol.meaning: A person whom everybody looks up to, such as a much-loved teacher or singer.
idol.clue: When the striker retired every club in the country called him an idol, and his old shirts filled the museum.

idyllic.meaning: So peaceful and lovely that it seems like a scene from a picture.
idyllic.clue: The tiny farmyard was utterly idyllic, with geese drifting past the gate and roses over the porch.

illicit.meaning: Against the law, so a thing done in that way is punishable.
illicit.clue: The site was found to be dealing in illicit goods, so police officers raided the warehouse in the early morning.

illuminate.meaning: Lighting up a dark room, or making a complicated idea easier for people to follow.
illuminate.clue: Two small lamps were enough to illuminate the whole shed once we moved them under the shelf.

illusory.meaning: Something that seems to be there or seems true but is only an impression.
illusory.clue: His sense of security was illusory, since the broken door lock was noticed within a few minutes.

imbalance.meaning: When the amounts or sizes of two parts do not match, so one side ends up heavier or bigger.
imbalance.clue: The two teams were so unequal in size that the coach picked the sides again before the match began.

imbroglio.meaning: A noisy quarrel or a muddled situation that has become hard to sort out.
imbroglio.clue: What began as a discussion about music turned into a full imbroglio, with two teachers shouting at once.

imminent.meaning: Certain to happen in a very short time, with no waiting left to do.
imminent.clue: When the storm warning came through, the staff knew the storm's arrival was imminent and cleared the yard.

immoral.meaning: Behaving in a way that is plainly wrong according to what most people believe is right.
immoral.clue: The head said that copying answers in an exam was wrong, and she expected every pupil to be honest instead.

immutable.meaning: Certain to stay exactly the same for all time, with no possibility of any change.
immutable.clue: The teacher said that the date of the school centenary was immutable, so nobody could move the celebration.

impassive.meaning: A face or manner that shows nothing, even when something shocking or upsetting has happened.
impassive.clue: He heard the news that his team had lost with an impassive stare, then walked quietly out of the hall.

impeccable.meaning: Absolutely correct and well made, with nothing at all wrong with any part.
impeccable.clue: Her knowledge of the subject was impeccable, and she answered every question without hesitating.

impecunious.meaning: So short of money that nothing beyond the barest necessities can be paid for.
impecunious.clue: As an impecunious student, Asha could not afford the art trip, so her form raised a collection for her.

impel.meaning: Making somebody feel they must go ahead, so that they have no real choice.
impel.clue: The terrible weather impelled the organisers to cancel the match and postpone it until April.

imperceptible.meaning: So tiny or so gradual that it is almost impossible to see or sense.
imperceptible.clue: There was an imperceptible rise in the ground, and the road ahead simply vanished behind it.

impermeable.meaning: Describing a material that does not let a single drop of water or draught pass through.
impermeable.clue: Even after two hours of driving rain, the boy's jacket was still dry when he took it off.

impetuous.meaning: Rushing to act the moment you feel something, before you have stopped to think it through.
impetuous.clue: His impetuous decision to swim out alone caused real panic on the beach that afternoon.

impinge.meaning: Affecting or interfering with something that was not meant to be disturbed.
impinge.clue: The new housing plan impinges on the playing field, and the school council has written a strong objection.

implausible.meaning: Not true enough to believe, usually because the details of the story cannot be right.
implausible.clue: His excuse about meeting a film star at the bus stop sounded so implausible that the class began to laugh.

implement.meaning: Once a new rule is implemented, everyone has to follow it instead of simply discussing it.
implement.clue: The school finally implemented its promise of free breakfast clubs, and every pupil who wanted one now gets breakfast.

implicate.meaning: The evidence did not prove he took the money, but it certainly connected him with the theft.
implicate.clue: The witness said she saw Dan near the bike sheds, which seemed to implicate him in the missing gold medals.

implicitly.meaning: By saying nothing about his age, the coach was quietly warning the boys to behave themselves.
implicitly.clue: When the head said the hall would be redecorated in September, he implicitly promised that our wall painting would survive.

impose.meaning: The council put a heavy fine on drivers who ignored the one-way street.
impose.clue: Our new landlord imposed a rule about pets, so we had to say goodbye to our goldfish.

impoverished.meaning: Poverty of this kind means a family cannot afford warm coats, glasses or even a hot meal.
impoverished.clue: After the flood, several families were left impoverished, and local charities handed out food parcels.

imprecise.meaning: The scientist checked her figures twice because the first set was rather rough and open to argument.
imprecise.clue: Our estimate of the crowd size was imprecise, so we guessed that about three hundred people had come.

impregnated.meaning: A vet can usually tell very early on whether an animal is carrying a litter of young.
impregnated.clue: The soil was impregnated with water after the storm, and our boots sank in at every step.

impromptu.meaning: Nobody had mentioned the two extra songs, so they were rather nerve-racking for us all.
impromptu.clue: Our singing teacher was ill, so Year Six gave an impromptu concert for the younger classes instead.

improvisation.meaning: This group enjoys making things up as they go along rather than following a fixed script.
improvisation.clue: When the power failed, the musicians filled the time with improvisation, and the crowd loved every second.

imprudent.meaning: It was a foolish choice to cross that wet playing field on your own after dark.
imprudent.clue: Taking a shortcut across the dual carriageway was imprudent, and Ben's bicycle ended up bent beyond repair.

inaccurate.meaning: Their figures were wrong, which meant the class raised far too little money for the charity.
inaccurate.clue: The website said the bus arrived at eight, but that information was inaccurate and we waited forty minutes.

inadequate.meaning: A thin coat was not enough protection when the rain started lashing the windows.
inadequate.clue: A hundred chairs proved inadequate for the hall, so two classes had to sit in the corridor.

inadvertently.meaning: She meant to close the gate but was carrying too much shopping and shut the door on the cat.
inadvertently.clue: Our class rep inadvertently deleted the whole homework list, so the teacher emailed it again.

inattentive.meaning: Children who do not listen often miss the instructions that everybody else has heard clearly.
inattentive.clue: The teacher asked everyone to stop being inattentive, as half the class had written the wrong date.

inaudible.meaning: The announcement was impossible to hear because somebody had muted the microphone.
inaudible.clue: Even from the back row, the tiny speaker made the headteacher's speech inaudible, so we guessed at the news.

incense.meaning: As the thin sticks burned, the sweet smoke curled slowly up towards the roof beams.
incense.clue: The incense in the church made the whole hall smell faintly of sandalwood and old wood.

incentive.meaning: A weekly payment for tidying up is a powerful reason for children to help without being asked.
incentive.clue: The promise of extra reading time was enough incentive for Femi to finish his library book.

incessant.meaning: The steady buzzing of that light fitting made it hard for anybody to concentrate on a page.
incessant.clue: The incessant knocking on the back door went on all evening, until Dad finally went down to look.

incidental.meaning: Selling a few cakes was a small extra, and the money went towards new sports kit.
incidental.clue: Charging for a hot drink was purely incidental to the main purpose of the trip.

incisive.meaning: Her question about our funding cut through the whole debate and settled it in seconds.
incisive.clue: The inspector's incisive questions made the headteacher pause before answering anything at all.

incite.meaning: Getting a group to turn on itself by deliberately pushing buttons is cruel and quite unfair.
incite.clue: A cruel message incited the whole year group to argue, and the staff had to sort it out.

incline.meaning: The grass at the top of the hill tilts gently towards the river at the bottom.
incline.clue: The floorboards incline towards the window, so a marble rolled all the way across the classroom.

inclusive.meaning: The new playground design has a quiet corner, which helps the children who need peace.
inclusive.clue: The teachers made sure the club was inclusive, so pupils from every year joined in the same club.

incoherent.meaning: After the long drive, my brother was too tired to give any sensible account of the day.
incoherent.clue: The witness gave such an incoherent story that the police could not decide what had happened.

incongruous.meaning: A bright glass box looks completely wrong beside two hundred years of old stonework.
incongruous.clue: His modern trainers looked incongruous with the rest of the smartly dressed team.

inconsolable.meaning: Even a week later she was crying, and no amount of ice cream could make her feel better.
inconsolable.clue: The youngest boy was inconsolable after losing his wrestling champion badge in the grass.

incontrovertible.meaning: The marks left at the scene were proof that no other person could have been in that room.
incontrovertible.clue: Three independent cameras filmed the theft, which made the case against the boys incontrovertible.

incorrigible.meaning: Three detentions in one week left the headteacher convinced that talking to him achieved nothing.
incorrigible.clue: Our form teacher laughed and said he was incorrigible, because no punishment ever changed his behaviour.

incumbent.meaning: Because the term is only a year, the school captain has to face a vote each September.
incumbent.clue: The incumbent, who had led the school council for a year, decided not to stand again.

incurable.meaning: The doctor said the damage to his knee was permanent, and that he would need a stick for life.
incurable.clue: Doctors explained that his asthma was incurable, and Mum learned exactly how to help during an attack.

indefatigable.meaning: A person like that will keep working hour after hour, and simply never seems to get worn down.
indefatigable.clue: The school's caretaker, indefatigable as ever, mowed the huge field before the weather turned.

indifferent.meaning: He barely reacted when he heard the final score, as though the whole match had meant nothing.
indifferent.clue: The judges seemed indifferent to our idea, and we never saw them again after that round.

indigenous.meaning: Clearing the woodland destroyed many plants that had grown there for thousands of years.
indigenous.clue: We learned that the bluebell is indigenous to British hedgerows, and it flowers in April every year.

indigent.meaning: The charity was set up to help the poorest families living in the oldest part of town.
indigent.clue: A young indigent boy was given a scholarship, and he later became the village doctor.

indignant.meaning: Nobody was pleased when the road was closed at the end of their street without any warning.
indignant.clue: Passengers became indignant when the railway company cancelled the service two minutes before departure.

indiscriminate.meaning: Spraying chemicals over the whole hillside killed the grass and the wild flowers together.
indiscriminate.clue: The council used indiscriminate weedkiller on the verges, and garden roses were destroyed too.

indomitable.meaning: Their refusal to be beaten carried them through three rounds of the competition.
indomitable.clue: Their goalkeeper was indomitable, and he saved two brilliant penalties in the last five minutes.

induce.meaning: The bright colours on the poster were enough to make her come and read the book.
induce.clue: Free pizza was enough to induce even the fussiest eaters to come along on Friday.

indulge.meaning: After the match she let us have a film and chips, which was very generous of her.
indulge.clue: His grandmother indulges him, so he always gets a huge present on his birthday.

inedible.meaning: The berries looked tempting, but the guide warned us that none of them were fit to eat.
inedible.clue: Our packed lunch included an inedible cheese sandwich, and nobody in Year Six could swallow a mouthful.

ineffable.meaning: Some kinds of music produce a feeling in the music room that no grown-up can really explain.
ineffable.clue: The choir's singing gave an ineffable feeling, and the whole hall was quiet afterwards.

ineffectual.meaning: The alarm was of no help at all, and the class slept through the whole drill.
ineffectual.clue: The wet wipes made no difference to the muddy floor, and every cleaning method we tried was ineffectual.

ineptitude.meaning: Getting the same task badly wrong again and again usually shows a total lack of training.
ineptitude.clue: The substitute cook's ineptitude showed when he boiled the vegetables until they turned to mush.

inequity.meaning: The charity exists to reduce the unfair gap between the richest and poorest areas of the city.
inequity.clue: The campaigners argued that the inequity between two schools in the town was unfair and wasteful.

inert.meaning: The engine sits quite still and does nothing at all until the key is turned.
inert.clue: Because the battery was flat, the robot sat inert on the carpet, waiting for new power.

inertia.meaning: Doing exactly the same thing for ten years had made the club very hard to change.
inertia.clue: The inertia of the old system meant that new ideas were ignored for years on end.

inevitably.meaning: As the weather was so bad all morning, the match was always going to be called off.
inevitably.clue: When the power cut during the test, everyone knew that the whole paper would inevitably have to be moved.

inexplicable.meaning: The children were frightened by the strange noises that kept coming from the cellar.
inexplicable.clue: Nobody could account for the inexplicable mess in the art room, and the caretaker looked worried.

infamous.meaning: That shop is remembered widely for burnt crusts and rude service from its owner.
infamous.clue: Our old caretaker was infamous for hiding the footballs, and every coach asked him about them.

infatuate.meaning: She was completely taken in with the new boy for weeks and barely noticed anything else.
infatuate.clue: The whole year became infatuated with the new chess set, and lessons were forgotten.

infer.meaning: You work something out for yourself by thinking about the clues you can see.
infer.clue: From the crumbs on the desk, I could infer that the boys had been eating in the library.

infernal.meaning: An old-fashioned word for something utterly dreadful, and also for anything to do with the underworld.
infernal.clue: The bus was late, the rain poured down and the whole journey felt absolutely infernal.

infiltrate.meaning: Nobody in the group realised that a newcomer had quietly made his way in.
infiltrate.clue: Our guide knew a secret way to infiltrate the castle so the tourists would not be spotted.

influence.meaning: What one person does ends up shaping the choices of a great many others.
influence.clue: His confident speech had a great influence on the team, who now believed they could win.

influential.meaning: Because of this person's standing, a great many others follow the example given.
influential.clue: The influential head teacher invited every class to enter the new writing competition.

infuriated.meaning: The person is so angry that they can hardly speak normally.
infuriated.clue: My brother was infuriated when he found out that his skateboard had been taken to school by mistake.

infuse.meaning: The new coach manages to pass a winning attitude right through the whole team.
infuse.clue: The coach tried to infuse confidence into the team before their first match of the season.

ingenious.meaning: Somebody has come up with a strikingly original solution to the problem.
ingenious.clue: Nell came up with an ingenious way of carrying her violin and her lunch on one bicycle.

ingrate.meaning: Kindness is repaid with complaints, arguments or complete silence.
ingrate.clue: After the choir sang at the care home, only one listener never said thank you, a real ingrate.

inhabit.meaning: That address is where they actually live, not merely somewhere they visit.
inhabit.clue: Three families inhabit the flats above the old bakery, just a stone's throw from school.

inhabitant.meaning: This creature is a native of the area described and never comes from anywhere else.
inhabitant.clue: Every inhabitant of our street joins the litter pick on the first Saturday of every month.

inhale.meaning: The breath travels inwards rather than outwards.
inhale.clue: Before the diving competition, Pip had to inhale deeply and hold his breath for a full minute.

inherent.meaning: Nobody put that quality there on purpose; it belongs to the thing by its very nature.
inherent.clue: There is an inherent risk in climbing without a helmet, which is why the club insists on safety gear.

initiate.meaning: A brand new scheme is being set under way, and everyone is invited to join in.
initiate.clue: Our head teacher will initiate a new reading club on Tuesday lunchtime for the younger children.

injustice.meaning: The rules have been bent in a way that gives one person an unfair deal.
injustice.clue: The pupils protested about the injustice of having to tidy up after the class who made the mess.

inkling.meaning: Something has been noticed, but the full picture is still missing.
inkling.clue: Dad had an inkling that we were planning a surprise party, so he pretended to be asleep.

innate.meaning: You were equipped with it long before you ever walked into a classroom.
innate.clue: Children have an innate ability to learn a second language, even if it seems difficult at first.

innovation.meaning: The method used here has never been tried in the school before.
innovation.clue: The innovation of a free lunch for every pupil has transformed what happens in our dining hall.

inopportune.meaning: Bad timing ruined something that would otherwise have worked well.
inopportune.clue: The head teacher made an inopportune announcement about homework just as the bell rang.

inquisitive.meaning: The class pushes past the facts given, wanting to know what lies behind them.
inquisitive.clue: Our inquisitive reporters asked sensible questions about the new library and took notes.

insane.meaning: The plan is so outlandishly silly that no adult would dream of trying it.
insane.clue: It was an insane decision to wear wellies to the fancy dress disco on Monday morning.

insatiable.meaning: No amount of what they are given seems to be enough.
insatiable.clue: His appetite for reading seems insatiable, and he has borrowed six books from the library this week.

insidious.meaning: Something bad creeps in where nobody is looking and only shows itself much later on.
insidious.clue: The insidious damp in the old gym has ruined three windows and nobody noticed until last month.

insight.meaning: The answer is not handed over; it grows out of long, patient thought.
insight.clue: Her insight into the town's history made the museum guide much more interesting to listen to.

insinuate.meaning: The speaker avoids the words, yet the sly remark still lands exactly as intended.
insinuate.clue: He was careful not to insinuate that anyone had copied the homework during the test.

insistent.meaning: However often the answer is no, the request is made all over again.
insistent.clue: After two polite emails, the school office became insistent and phoned my parents directly.

insomnia.meaning: Hours pass while the body is tired and the mind refuses to switch off.
insomnia.clue: Worrying about the entrance exam gave her insomnia, and she felt exhausted all day.

inspire.meaning: The pupil is given the confidence to attempt something better than before.
inspire.clue: A visit from an author can inspire the class to write a story for the competition.

instigate.meaning: One careless person sets off a chain of events that others then carry on.
instigate.clue: Careless whispers in the back row can instigate an argument that soon spreads across the year group.

instil.meaning: A lasting attitude is built up in someone day after day, without any force.
instil.clue: Reading aloud to his younger sister every night helped instil in him a real love of stories.

instructive.meaning: Children come away having picked up a fact they had not known before.
instructive.clue: Our visit to the old railway museum was so instructive that the class sketched the signal box.

insufferable.meaning: Nobody in the room can stand it for even a minute.
insufferable.clue: His insufferable tapping of the pen during the test made the rest of the hall sigh.

insular.meaning: Their opinions stop at the edge of their own neighbourhood.
insular.clue: Their insular attitude to visitors changed once the school began to welcome exchange pupils from other countries.

insurgent.meaning: The people have taken up weapons to fight the rulers they refuse to obey.
insurgent.clue: Our geography teacher explained that an insurgent takes up arms against the government while a protester only demonstrates.

insurmountable.meaning: No amount of extra effort or extra time will ever get the task finished.
insurmountable.clue: The team thought the final round was an insurmountable challenge, yet they still finished second.

intact.meaning: Despite years of neglect, every piece is still exactly as it was made.
intact.clue: Amazingly, the ancient coins were still intact after five hundred years buried in the ground.

intangible.meaning: You know that the quality is there, but you cannot see it or put your finger on it.
intangible.clue: Trust between teammates is an intangible quality, yet it decides who really wins matches.

integral.meaning: The whole thing collapses if this part is taken away.
integral.clue: Regular revision is integral to success, so the library stays open every Thursday evening.

integrity.meaning: The person tells the truth and refuses to cheat, even when nobody is watching.
integrity.clue: A person of real integrity admits when they have made a mistake, even if nobody else noticed.

intense.meaning: Nothing about it is mild; the heat or the emotion is turned up very high.
intense.clue: The intense heat in the hall made everyone sleepy during the long assembly.

intention.meaning: A decision has been made in advance, even though the work has not begun.
intention.clue: I had every intention of finishing my project, but I spent the evening playing instead.

intercede.meaning: Somebody steps in to plead with an angry party and settle the trouble.
intercede.clue: Our head teacher chose to intercede with the angry parent, and the argument ended calmly.

intermittent.meaning: There is a spell of activity, then nothing at all for a while, and then it returns.
intermittent.clue: The rain came in intermittent bursts, so we waited under the tree for the showers to end.

intervene.meaning: Control of the situation passes from those involved to somebody else.
intervene.clue: Our dinner lady will intervene whenever two pupils begin arguing in the dining hall.

intimate.meaning: What is being discussed would never be said in front of the whole class.
intimate.clue: She wrote an intimate diary about her feelings, and she never let anybody else read it.

intimidate.meaning: Even without a word being said, the glare is enough to make people comply.
intimidate.clue: A glaring stare can intimidate the youngest pupils into sitting silently during assembly.

intractable.meaning: Every solution tried so far has led nowhere, and nobody can see a way through.
intractable.clue: The head teacher admitted that the problem of phone use in lessons was intractable without new rules.

intransigent.meaning: Offers, threats and reasoning make no impression; the position is fixed.
intransigent.clue: The captain was intransigent about playing in the rain, so the match was postponed.

introspective.meaning: Rather than blaming others, the pupil turns the searchlight on their own conduct.
introspective.clue: After the play she became introspective, quietly wondering whether she had said the right thing.

introvert.meaning: Being asked to address the whole school is the last thing this pupil enjoys.
introvert.clue: As an introvert, Sam enjoyed the library best of all and liked reading there on his own.

intuition.meaning: Sometimes you simply know that something is about to happen, without being able to explain why.
intuition.clue: Her sharp intuition told her that the new boy in our class could not be trusted.

intuitive.meaning: A method or tool that feels so obvious that you can use it straight away.
intuitive.clue: The website has an intuitive design, so even beginners can order tickets without any help.

inundate.meaning: So much water or so many things arrived at once that the place could not cope.
inundate.clue: Winter storms can inundate the field, and the whole lower pitch ends up under water.

invalid.meaning: It cannot be accepted or used, because no rule gives it the right to stand.
invalid.clue: The referee said the goal was invalid because the ball had clearly crossed the line beforehand.

invaluable.meaning: Something that helps you so much that you could never say what it is worth.
invaluable.clue: Grandad's old advice was invaluable when I had to choose my options for secondary school.

investigate.meaning: You ask questions and gather facts in order to understand something properly.
investigate.clue: The head teacher agreed to investigate the complaints made by three parents about the trip.

irascible.meaning: Someone who loses their temper over the tiniest thing.
irascible.clue: Our caretaker was irascible, losing his temper over tiny things, so we nicknamed him Short Fuse.

ire.meaning: Deep, hot anger, the sort that makes you want to shout at somebody.
ire.clue: The headmaster's ire was clear when he saw graffiti sprayed across the changing room wall.

ironic.meaning: Someone who means the opposite of what their words appear to say.
ironic.clue: After losing the final, he said he was delighted to have lost, an ironic remark nobody believed.

irrational.meaning: Someone who does not think things through and acts on whatever enters their head.
irrational.clue: It was an irrational decision to walk home alone through the park in the dark.

irrelevant.meaning: Not connected with the matter, and therefore not worth worrying about.
irrelevant.clue: Half his answer was irrelevant, so the examiner could not award any marks.

irreproachable.meaning: Every part of it is so correct and decent that nobody can find anything wrong.
irreproachable.clue: Her record during the year was irreproachable, so she was trusted with the younger class.

irresistible.meaning: So attractive that you find it completely impossible to say no to it.
irresistible.clue: The smell of fresh bread outside the bakery was irresistible, and we all bought rolls.

irreverence.meaning: Speaking or behaving without the respect that something deserves.
irreverence.clue: Her irreverence towards the war memorial annoyed the headmaster, who asked for an apology.

itinerary.meaning: The full plan of where you are going and what you will do each day.
itinerary.clue: Our itinerary packed in four museums, but we managed only one before the rain began.

jargon.meaning: Special vocabulary that only people in a certain job or group really use.
jargon.clue: The instructions were full of jargon, so I rang the helpline for a simpler explanation.

jaunty.meaning: Happy and full of bounce, as though nothing in the world worried you.
jaunty.clue: He walked into the interview jaunty and smiling, and left with three offers.

jeopardise.meaning: To put a plan, a job or a life in danger of going wrong.
jeopardise.clue: Chasing that ball into the road could jeopardise our team's place in the final.

jittery.meaning: Feeling jumpy and slightly wobbly, usually because you are worried or excited.
jittery.clue: The pupils became jittery as the results were read out, and nobody dared move.

jocular.meaning: Someone who loves to joke about things and keep everybody laughing.
jocular.clue: At the prize-giving the headmaster was jocular, pretending to search for the envelope.

joyous.meaning: So happy and excited that everything seems wonderful and bright.
joyous.clue: There was a joyous cheer when the school choir was told it had won the competition.

judicious.meaning: Making sensible choices after thinking things over properly.
judicious.clue: The judicious use of colours made our tiny classroom feel calm and much bigger.

just.meaning: Nobody is favoured, and every single person is treated in the same correct way.
just.clue: The decision seemed just, because the same rule was applied to every player that morning.

justice.meaning: A fair result, in which a wrong is punished and nobody is cheated.
justice.clue: When the thief admitted the damage, the owner felt that justice had finally been done.

justification.meaning: The good reasons somebody gives to show that what they did was the right thing.
justification.clue: He offered no justification for arriving late, and the class took a dim view.

juxtapose.meaning: Putting two contrasting things together so that the differences stand out.
juxtapose.clue: The poster designer chose to juxtapose a luxury hotel with a crowded hostel, making a point about wealth.

keen.meaning: Feeling very excited and ready to take part, or very quick to learn.
keen.clue: She was keen to join the swimming club, so she filled in the form that same day.

labour.meaning: Tiring work that uses up your strength and leaves you exhausted.
labour.clue: Years of labour went into restoring the old stone wall behind the church hall.

labyrinth.meaning: A complicated twisting set of ways, so that you easily lose your direction.
labyrinth.clue: The catacombs are a vast labyrinth, and our guide knew every single turning passage.

laconic.meaning: Someone who says as little as possible, giving you only a few short words.
laconic.clue: His laconic reply was two words, and the head of year smiled and moved on.

lame.meaning: Hobbling along because one leg is weak or hurts when weight is put on it.
lame.clue: The old pony went lame, so the vet came at once to check its back leg.

lassitude.meaning: That thick, drooping tiredness that comes from having nothing to look forward to.
lassitude.clue: A lassitude settled over the class on the hot Friday afternoon, and nobody picked up a book.

latent.meaning: Still there inside, but out of sight until something brings it out.
latent.clue: His latent talent for drawing only appeared when the art teacher noticed his sketchbook.

latter.meaning: The one of the two that is spoken of second, or nearer the end.
latter.clue: Of the two twins, the latter spoke French while her sister spoke only English.

lethargic.meaning: Too tired and flat to move or think properly, like a slow snail.
lethargic.clue: After the long journey he was too lethargic to play, and simply watched television.

lethargy.meaning: A deep, heavy tiredness that makes it hard to move or even to think.
lethargy.clue: Deep lethargy followed the flu, and she needed two hours to wake up properly.

levitate.meaning: To stay up in the air unsupported, floating instead of falling.
levitate.clue: The magician claimed he could levitate, but the audience sat quietly and waited.

levity.meaning: A moment of fun and joking even when everybody around you is serious.
levity.clue: The head of year's levity broke the tension, and soon everyone was laughing again.

liberal.meaning: Happy to give freely, and to accept views different from your own.
liberal.clue: The school took a liberal approach, letting pupils wear whatever they liked on non-uniform days.

liberty.meaning: Being free to act, think and speak for yourself without anyone ruling you.
liberty.clue: The prisoners won their liberty after three years of appealing against the decision.

lieu.meaning: Used when one thing is given or done to take the place of another.
lieu.clue: The team gave a spare shirt in lieu of the one lost, and the match went ahead.

limb.meaning: One of the arms or legs that come out of a person's body.
limb.clue: He stretched out one limb and knocked the whole row of pencils off the desk.

limit.meaning: The point beyond which you cannot go, or the largest amount you may have.
limit.clue: There is a limit on how many sweets each child may bring into the hall.

listless.meaning: So without energy that you cannot be bothered to do anything at all.
listless.clue: The heat made everyone listless, so the whole team lay on the grass.

litigation.meaning: A legal fight in which people take their disagreement to a judge to settle it.
litigation.clue: Litigation over the shared fence lasted two years and drained the neighbours' savings.

lodge.meaning: To state a complaint officially, so that someone in charge can deal with it.
lodge.clue: Several families decided to lodge complaints about the noise from the late club.

loiter.meaning: Hanging about in a place when you ought to be moving along.
loiter.clue: Groups of pupils loiter outside the gates, so the caretaker asks them to move on.

loneliness.meaning: That aching sense of missing other people when you have nobody around.
loneliness.clue: To beat her loneliness, Bella joined the drama club and made several close friends.

loquacious.meaning: Someone who talks constantly and has plenty to say about almost everything.
loquacious.clue: Our new neighbour is wonderfully loquacious, chatting happily right through every journey home.

loyal.meaning: Staying true to someone or something and standing by them when things go wrong.
loyal.clue: The team stayed loyal to their captain even after the terrible run of defeats.

lucrative.meaning: A lucrative job or contract pays far more than most, so people compete hard to get it.
lucrative.clue: She took a lucrative job in banking because the salary was far better than teaching.

ludicrous.meaning: A ludicrous idea is so silly that no sensible person would ever take it seriously.
ludicrous.clue: Our team wore huge feathered hats for the play, and they looked absolutely ludicrous on the stage.

lulled.meaning: To lull a person or a crowd is to help them relax and stop paying attention.
lulled.clue: Her mother's soft singing lulled the little boy to sleep, so he never heard the thunder.

luminous.meaning: Something luminous produces light of its own, just as a lamp or a star does.
luminous.clue: The librarian found a luminous green ball in the attic, and it lit up the whole room.

lustrous.meaning: Lustrous hair or metal has a glossy surface that reflects light in a deep, rich way.
lustrous.clue: The candidate shook hands with the headteacher, and her lustrous silver hair caught everyone's eye.

magnanimous.meaning: A magnanimous person returns good for evil and shares whatever they have.
magnanimous.clue: When a rival side complained about the umpire, the captain was magnanimous and said nothing at all.

magnate.meaning: A magnate has built a huge company and holds enormous power over that industry.
magnate.clue: The newspapers are owned by a publishing magnate who also runs three television channels.

magnetic.meaning: A magnetic person or idea pulls everyone towards it, rather as a magnet pulls iron.
magnetic.clue: Our new pupil had a magnetic personality, and by lunchtime every child in the form room wanted to talk to her.

magnitude.meaning: To judge the magnitude of a problem, people ask how big and how serious it is.
magnitude.clue: Nobody understood the magnitude of the task until they saw how many pages still needed writing.

malevolent.meaning: A malevolent character enjoys seeing other people suffer and plots to make things worse.
malevolent.clue: The story described a malevolent witch who tricked farmers and frightened every child in the parish.

malleable.meaning: Malleable metal can be reshaped without cracking, which makes it useful for making things.
malleable.clue: The warm clay was so malleable that the youngest child in the nursery reshaped it into a dinosaur.

masculinity.meaning: Masculinity is a set of ideas about how a man should behave, and those ideas have changed a lot.
masculinity.clue: Our topic on masculinity looked at how boys and girls are expected to behave in different ways.

maverick.meaning: A maverick thinks for themselves and is willing to disagree with everybody else.
maverick.clue: Joining the school play was a maverick choice for Finn, who usually preferred football at the weekend.

measly.meaning: A measly meal or wage is far too small to satisfy a person properly.
measly.clue: The winning side was given a measly slice of cake after the final, which caused a few complaints.

meddle.meaning: To meddle means to interfere in things that are really none of your business.
meddle.clue: If you meddle in your brother's plans, you will make him change his mind and worry more.

mediate.meaning: To mediate is to act as a fair go-between so that people stop arguing and reach a settlement.
mediate.clue: A teacher had to mediate when two friends fell out over a borrowed pencil case in the changing room.

mediocrity.meaning: Mediocrity describes a performance or plan that is neither good nor bad but simply uninspiring.
mediocrity.clue: The annual show suffered from mediocrity this year, since none of the sketches made the audience laugh.

melody.meaning: A melody is a group of notes arranged so that they sound sweet together.
melody.clue: At the concert, a boy played a slow melody on the violin, and the whole hall fell silent.

menacing.meaning: A menacing stranger is one who frightens you, because they seem ready to attack.
menacing.clue: A menacing man hung around the gates, so the caretaker kept a careful watch over the playground.

mercurial.meaning: A mercurial performer is full of sudden energy and acts differently from one day to the next.
mercurial.clue: Our mercurial goalie saves brilliantly one minute, then lets in an easy goal the very next.

mercy.meaning: A judge showed mercy by giving the young offender a lighter punishment than she deserved.
mercy.clue: The rabbit pleaded for mercy, and the farmer decided to let it go rather than kill it for supper.

mere.meaning: If a win was mere luck, then there was no real skill behind it, only chance.
mere.clue: Winning the school prize was mere luck, because Jonas had not revised for a single evening all term.

mesmerise.meaning: A good storyteller can mesmerise a crowd so that nobody in the hall makes a sound.
mesmerise.clue: Card tricks like that can mesmerise an audience of any age, and the teachers forgot to clap.

methodical.meaning: A methodical worker finishes each stage of a job carefully before starting the next one.
methodical.clue: He followed a methodical plan in the study room, ticking off each topic on his checklist before resting.

metropolis.meaning: Millions of people travel into a metropolis every morning to work in its offices and shops.
metropolis.clue: On the exchange trip we crossed to a busy metropolis, where the streets were crowded from dawn until midnight.

mettle.meaning: Climbing the icy mountain in a whiteout needed real nerve, but she still reached the top.
mettle.clue: Even though his knee was injured, Tomas showed real mettle and finished the cross-country race.

milestone.meaning: Getting her driving licence was a real milestone, because she could finally travel alone.
milestone.clue: Winning the county swimming badge was the highlight of his year and a milestone he will not forget.

misanthrope.meaning: Once famous for his kindness, he turned into a bitter misanthrope who avoided everybody.
misanthrope.clue: The character in the novel is a misanthrope who never speaks to a soul and lives alone in the hills.

misapprehend.meaning: If you misapprehend the instructions, you will make mistakes and have to start again.
misapprehend.clue: The guide may misapprehend the question and explain the wrong part of the syllabus, leaving the class confused.

mischief.meaning: A class full of mischief keeps the teacher laughing and sighing at the same time.
mischief.clue: Their mischief began when one brother tied the other boy's shoelaces together during assembly.

miserly.meaning: A miserly old man counted every penny twice and never bought himself a treat.
miserly.clue: A miserly old landlord kept the heating off in winter, so the tenants had to wash in cold water.

misnomer.meaning: People argue that a misleading word is a misnomer and ask for it to be changed.
misnomer.clue: The sign called the shop a bakery, but it sold nothing but greetings cards, which was a real misnomer.

misogynist.meaning: A misogynist is convinced that one sex is better than the other and acts on that belief.
misogynist.clue: The film showed a misogynist character who insults half the people he works with and expects everyone to obey him without question.

misspent.meaning: To misspent a holiday means to fill it with unhelpful things and get nothing from it.
misspent.clue: He misspent his whole Saturday afternoon on computer games, so his homework was still undone.

mitigate.meaning: Quick repairs can mitigate the danger of a fall, but the best plan is to keep floors clear.
mitigate.clue: Heavy rain and a broken drain flooded the gym, and sandbags helped to mitigate the damage.

moderate.meaning: A moderate amount of revision helps, but three hours in one evening will not.
moderate.clue: The headteacher asked for a moderate increase in fees, which the parents' group welcomed with relief.

modernise.meaning: Deciding to modernise a building means replacing what is old and worn with new fittings.
modernise.clue: Our school will modernise its computer room next term, replacing the old desktop machines with tablets for everybody.

modest.meaning: A modest winner thanks her team and says nothing about her own part in it.
modest.clue: The charity asked for a modest sum, so we raised two hundred pounds instead of twenty.

mogul.meaning: Owning several newspapers and television stations makes a person a real mogul.
mogul.clue: The article explained that a media mogul now owns several channels, newspapers and film studios.

mollify.meaning: The coach mollified the angry parent by apologising for the team's poor performance.
mollify.clue: A few gentle words from the teacher can mollify a furious boy, and soon he is ready to talk again.

momentous.meaning: The announcement of peace was a momentous occasion for a country that had been at war for years.
momentous.clue: It was a momentous day when the old primary school finally closed after serving the neighbourhood for ninety years.

monochrome.meaning: Old black and white photographs are monochrome, so everything in them looks grey and unreal.
monochrome.clue: The pupil chose a monochrome poster for the project, drawing her cat in black ink on white paper.

monologue.meaning: A monologue is a talk in which one performer never shares the stage with anybody.
monologue.clue: The comedy show ended with a long monologue, and even the bored audience stayed quiet.

monotonous.meaning: A monotonous task keeps repeating in exactly the same way until it wears you out.
monotonous.clue: Three hours of monotonous music left several pupils yawning by the end of the assembly.

monumental.meaning: Building the tower took eleven years, and the finished structure now stands in a vast open square.
monumental.clue: The museum's new staircase is a monumental piece of engineering, wide enough for a whole class to walk up together.

moratorium.meaning: The council placed a moratorium on the new road, meaning nothing could be built for two years.
moratorium.clue: During the building work there was a moratorium on traffic, so no lorry could pass down our road.

morose.meaning: A morose person withdraws from everybody and answers questions in a flat voice.
morose.clue: After losing the final, he sat in the corner wearing a morose expression and refused to speak.

mortal.meaning: As a mortal being, she knew she would not live for ever, so she planned carefully.
mortal.clue: The old tale tells of a mortal knight who could be hurt, unlike the gods who watched over the battle.

mournful.meaning: A mournful song or face tells other people that somebody is upset or has been hurt.
mournful.clue: The slow music played during the funeral, and even the youngest children in the hall were mournful.

mundane.meaning: A mundane job is dull and unchanging, and it rarely brings excitement or a surprise.
mundane.clue: The assembly discussed a mundane topic such as how to store the sports kit in the cupboard.

munificence.meaning: She became known for her munificence, and gave quietly to causes nobody else would support.
munificence.clue: Her munificence astonished everyone, because she paid for new books for every class in the school.

muted.meaning: His answer was so quiet that people at the back of the hall had to lean forward.
muted.clue: The speaker's voice was so muted that we leaned forward to hear every word of the announcement.

mysterious.meaning: A strange noise came from the empty corridor, but nobody could work out what was making it.
mysterious.clue: The mysterious letter had no address, and my postman said it had been pushed through the door.

mystify.meaning: The wizard's tricks mystified the audience, because nobody could see how the rabbits appeared.
mystify.clue: Rather than admitting the error, the manager chose to mystify everyone by changing the dates on the report.

nauseating.meaning: The smell of the old milk made us feel sick, and my sister quickly shut the fridge door.
nauseating.clue: A nauseating smell came from the science lab, so the door was opened and everyone stood back.

neat.meaning: He has such neat handwriting that even his hurried notes are easy for us to read.
neat.clue: In our form, each pupil must keep a neat folder, so papers and photographs do not get lost.

nefarious.meaning: The judge described the thief as nefarious, saying he had deliberately ruined hundreds of families.
nefarious.clue: Police warned us about a nefarious group who cheat tourists by selling fake tickets.

negate.meaning: By challenging the witness, the lawyer hoped to cancel out the story his client had told.
negate.clue: The witness changed her story, and the defence hoped this would negate the case against her.

negotiate.meaning: The two classes negotiated a longer break time instead of arguing about it for weeks.
negotiate.clue: Our head boy was sent to negotiate with the chefs about the cost of the end of year party.

nemesis.meaning: The tall forward gave us trouble in every match, scoring three goals each time we met.
nemesis.clue: Nobody in our club could forget our nemesis, who beat us twice in the same week.

nobility.meaning: It was her nobility that persuaded the angry crowd to forgive him after the terrible mistake.
nobility.clue: Even in defeat, the captain showed real nobility, congratulating the other team warmly.

nomadic.meaning: The family travelled with their goats, moving from village to village every summer of her childhood.
nomadic.clue: My aunt lived a nomadic life, packing her books before moving to a new island every year.

nominal.meaning: Our form has a nominal head teacher, but she works in another school on Friday afternoons.
nominal.clue: He was only a nominal member of the committee, so he was never asked to vote on anything.

nonchalant.meaning: She acted as if the surprise result had been planned all along, and nobody minded.
nonchalant.clue: He was nonchalant about the lost homework, simply shrugging and asking for a fresh sheet.

nonentity.meaning: As a new reporter, he went from being ignored to being quoted within a single week.
nonentity.clue: Without the captain's courage, the whole team would have been a nonentity by the final whistle.

nourishment.meaning: The cupboard held so little that the youngest children had to be fed by their neighbours.
nourishment.clue: Children who skip breakfast often lack the nourishment they need to grow and concentrate.

noxious.meaning: We were told the gas was poisonous, so everyone left the laboratory at once.
noxious.clue: The noxious fumes from the spill made the firefighters tie masks over their faces.

nuance.meaning: Two small differences between the original words and their new versions carry a real warning.
nuance.clue: My teacher spotted the nuance straight away, asking whether the word meant a polite lie or a real promise.

obdurate.meaning: The landlord would not budge, and kept the same price even after all our repairs.
obdurate.clue: Even after the head waited an hour, the obdurate caretaker still refused to open the gate.

obfuscate.meaning: Too many long words can cloud a simple idea and hide what is really being said.
obfuscate.clue: Rather than answer plainly, the spokesman used long words to obfuscate the facts of the case.

objection.meaning: My only worry about the plan is that it will cost more than the school can afford.
objection.clue: Several parents raised an objection when the swimming lessons were cut from the timetable.

oblique.meaning: He gave such an evasive answer that we still did not know what he actually thought.
oblique.clue: The sign had been placed at such an oblique angle that passing drivers missed it completely.

obliterate.meaning: The storm flattened the old pier, leaving nothing but broken wood along the beach.
obliterate.clue: Firemen warned that the blaze could obliterate the old hall if the wind turned our way.

obnoxious.meaning: His constant shouting across the corridor made everybody in year six furious.
obnoxious.clue: The obnoxious boy pushed past everybody in the queue and then blamed someone else.

obscure.meaning: An obscure poem on page forty is actually the best thing in the whole anthology.
obscure.clue: The atlas was so obscure that we had never heard of half those countries before opening it.

obsequious.meaning: She found his manner unbearable, because she knew that he never meant a word of it.
obsequious.clue: The obsequious new boy agreed with everything the head said, even the silly rules.

obsession.meaning: Her obsession with the violin meant that she practised every evening without fail.
obsession.clue: His obsession with old stamps has filled three drawers and completely taken over his free time.

obstreperous.meaning: Two badly behaved Year Six boys were sent to the head's office for shouting at each other.
obstreperous.clue: One obstreperous pupil shouted over the whole assembly, and everyone turned to stare.

odious.meaning: The head called the graffiti hateful and promised that it would be cleaned up that week.
odious.clue: Everyone agreed the joke was odious, and the class asked the writer to apologise.

odour.meaning: A damp smell drifted up from the cellar, so we opened every window in the house.
odour.clue: The strong odour of the paint was so bad that we had to leave the hall.

officious.meaning: His habit of reporting every small thing to the head made him very unpopular with staff.
officious.clue: The officious monitor told the head about every talk in the corridor, which made people stop talking.

ominous.meaning: The dark clouds and the empty beach felt threatening, so we turned back towards home.
ominous.clue: There was an ominous knock at the door just as the exams were due to start.

omit.meaning: Check your answers carefully, because a single missing line can cost you marks.
omit.clue: Please do not omit the date from your form, or the office cannot file it.

onerous.meaning: Clearing the yard was such hard work that we asked older pupils to help us.
onerous.clue: Preparing the summer play was more onerous than we expected, and half the costumes did not fit.

onslaught.meaning: The team weathered a furious attack in the second half and still kept hold of their lead.
onslaught.clue: Without help from our keeper, we could not have survived that onslaught of shots.

oppose.meaning: Most parents were against the idea of pupils using their phones in the dining hall.
oppose.clue: Local parents gathered to oppose the proposal, worried that the field would be sold for housing.

opt.meaning: You can decide not to join the trip, but you must still come to the assembly.
opt.clue: You can opt to join the chess club this term, but nobody will mind if you say no.

optimist.meaning: My sister is the sort of person who believes she will win the competition before it starts.
optimist.clue: Despite the rain, the optimist in our class still believes the sports day will go ahead.

optional.meaning: Wearing a tie on Friday is a matter of choice, so nobody minds if you come without one.
optional.clue: Choosing a house in the history project is optional, but everyone must write about the war.

orchestrate.meaning: Our head organised a charity week, and every class found its own way to help.
orchestrate.clue: It is hard to believe one girl could orchestrate a concert for three hundred people without any help.

origin.meaning: Nobody has ever explained the strange silver key, or the person who left it under the steps.
origin.clue: Nobody knows the origin of the strange silver key found under the school steps.

oscillate.meaning: The needle kept jumping, and my reading changed every few seconds of the lesson.
oscillate.clue: The temperature will oscillate between freezing and warm, so nobody can decide what to wear.

outrageous.meaning: The council called the rent rises shocking and promised to look at them again.
outrageous.clue: It was outrageous that the school bus had not turned up, leaving us stranded.

overbearing.meaning: His bossy manner made the younger children avoid the cloakroom altogether at lunchtime.
overbearing.clue: An overbearing prefect simply ordered us out of the hall without asking why we were there.

pacifist.meaning: He refuses to join any group that trains people to fight, whatever people say about him.
pacifist.clue: Our pacifist speaker explained why he would not join the army, and the hall stayed silent.

pacify.meaning: A few calm words from the head teacher settled the furious queue outside the door.
pacify.clue: The dinner supervisor managed to pacify the queue after the pizza ran out part way through.

pact.meaning: The two houses made a formal promise, agreeing to share one tent at the camping trip.
pact.clue: The council and the parents signed a pact that promised more parking near the school gates.

palpable.meaning: The strain between the two teams was plain for all to see, even out in the playground.
palpable.clue: The change in her voice was palpable, and we all knew she had heard the bad news.

pamper.meaning: They gave the dog so much attention that he now expects his dinner at six every evening.
pamper.clue: We must not pamper the class hamster, or it will expect a full dinner every day.

panacea.meaning: Long holidays are no lasting answer, and teachers know the same problems return every September.
panacea.clue: An hour of reading is useful, but it is no panacea for a pupil who has not eaten.

panache.meaning: To do something with panache is to do it in a dazzlingly confident style that turns every eye towards you.
panache.clue: With great panache, the young chef carried the silver platter into the crowded hall and bowed.

panic.meaning: Sudden wild fear that takes over your senses and makes you forget how to think clearly.
panic.clue: When the power failed in the dark hall, the whole class fell into panic and rushed for the exit.

parable.meaning: A parable tells a story whose ending makes people think about how they ought to behave.
parable.clue: The teacher told a parable about a boy who shared his lunch with a hungry stranger.

paradigm.meaning: When something is a paradigm, it sets the standard that later examples of the same kind follow.
paradigm.clue: For years our school timetable followed the same paradigm, with every lesson starting on the hour.

paradox.meaning: A paradox says something that seems impossible, yet it can still turn out to be true.
paradox.clue: It seems a paradox that the busiest shop had the fewest customers of the entire morning.

paragon.meaning: A paragon is somebody so good at something that everyone would like to be exactly like them.
paragon.clue: Our headteacher, who never wasted a minute, was a paragon of efficiency that we all tried to copy.

parallel.meaning: Lines that are parallel carry on together for ever, and no amount of stretching will ever make them meet.
parallel.clue: The two railway lines ran parallel for miles before the new tunnel finally brought them together.

paraphrase.meaning: To paraphrase is to put a speaker's words into your own writing while keeping the same sense.
paraphrase.clue: The headteacher's announcement was long, so we were asked to paraphrase it in our own words.

parsimony.meaning: A person who shows parsimony refuses to spend or share anything, even when they have plenty.
parsimony.clue: Their neighbour's parsimony was obvious: she still carried the same lunch box to school after ten years.

partial.meaning: Something partial is not finished or not done in full, so a part of it is still missing.
partial.clue: Because the storm had washed away part of the cliff path, we only had a partial view of the bay.

pathetic.meaning: A pathetic effort is so weak and badly done that people might laugh at it or feel sorry for it.
pathetic.clue: The team's goal was pathetic, sailing into the net after only three minutes of play.

pedantic.meaning: A pedantic person corrects tiny unimportant details instead of getting on with the main job.
pedantic.clue: Miss Reid became pedantic about the exact wording of the rules, so we wasted ten minutes before starting.

penchant.meaning: A penchant for something means you enjoy it more than most other things and seek it often.
penchant.clue: My sister has a penchant for collecting old postcards, and her shelf is now completely full of them.

perchance.meaning: A writer uses perchance when they are not certain that something is true or will happen.
perchance.clue: Perchance the parcel will arrive tomorrow, although nobody has told us when it was posted.

perfidious.meaning: Someone perfidious pretends to be a friend while secretly working against the people who help them.
perfidious.clue: The perfidious guide led us three miles in the wrong direction and laughed at our confusion.

perjury.meaning: To commit perjury is to swear on the Bible in a court and then deliberately tell a lie.
perjury.clue: The driver was charged with perjury after the court proved that his account of the crash had changed.

permit.meaning: To be given leave to do something, so that you may go ahead because someone in charge has agreed.
permit.clue: The headteacher said she would permit us to use the corridor for our treasure hunt after lunch.

pernicious.meaning: Something pernicious works away quietly, harming people or plants a little at a time.
pernicious.clue: The guide warned us that this weed was pernicious, spreading quietly across the whole lawn in summer.

perpetual.meaning: If something is perpetual it never pauses, so it lasts for as long as you keep watching.
perpetual.clue: Their argument about the football fixture went on for ages, seeming as perpetual as a dripping tap.

perplex.meaning: A question that perplexes you keeps you puzzling, because you cannot work out the answer.
perplex.clue: The strange instructions in the treasure hunt perplexed our team so much that we asked the teacher.

perseverance.meaning: Perseverance means carrying on with a job long after it stops being easy or fun.
perseverance.clue: Her perseverance won the prize, as she had practised every evening for six months without a single break.

perturb.meaning: To perturb someone is to put a small worry in their mind, which then lingers there.
perturb.clue: I was a little perturbed when a noisy class appeared outside the door during our assembly practice.

peruse.meaning: To peruse something means to read it slowly and thoroughly rather than looking over it quickly.
peruse.clue: We had to peruse the timetable carefully to find the coach that leaves at four o'clock.

pervasive.meaning: A smell described as pervasive gets into every corner and follows you from room to room.
pervasive.clue: The smell of damp was pervasive in the old shed, hiding in the corners and clinging to our clothes.

pessimist.meaning: A pessimist always looks for bad news and expects good things to go wrong.
pessimist.clue: Every pessimist in our class predicted a terrible end to the trip before we had even left school.

petulant.meaning: A petulant person pouts, snaps and complains at small problems instead of brushing them aside.
petulant.clue: The referee grew petulant after the third argument, snapping at the players instead of giving a decision.

phenomena.meaning: Several things that can be watched and measured, such as shadows, storms or plants growing.
phenomena.clue: Class four spent a whole morning recording phenomena such as shadows, frost and rippling water in the garden.

philosophical.meaning: A philosophical question asks why something is the way it is, not just how to do it.
philosophical.clue: Her philosophical answer about why leaves change colour silenced the whole class for a moment.

phlegmatic.meaning: Someone phlegmatic stays quiet and steady, however exciting the moment happens to be.
phlegmatic.clue: Despite the crowd cheering for the final goal, the goalkeeper stayed phlegmatic and walked back slowly.

picturesque.meaning: A picturesque village has such pretty old buildings that you feel you are looking at a painting.
picturesque.clue: The picturesque harbour was full of fishing boats, and every cottage had flowers in the window.

pining.meaning: To pine for somebody is to miss them so much that you keep thinking about them.
pining.clue: The little dog spent the whole afternoon pining at the gate for its owner.

pitfall.meaning: A pitfall is a problem that you do not see coming until you have walked straight into it.
pitfall.clue: Not checking the tide times was a real pitfall, and the sand was already covered in water.

plagiarise.meaning: Plagiarism is cheating, because the pupil who takes the words is not doing the thinking.
plagiarise.clue: A pupil who plagiarises a paragraph from a book will lose marks, however perfect the words are.

plausible.meaning: A plausible story hangs together nicely, so you believe it until you check the details.
plausible.clue: His excuse for missing the match was plausible, so the teacher believed every word he said.

pleasing.meaning: Something pleasing makes other people satisfied or delighted, such as a good report or neat handwriting.
pleasing.clue: The choir's result was pleasing, and the audience clapped for a full minute afterwards.

pleasurable.meaning: A pleasurable experience gives you a warm, happy feeling that you enjoy long afterwards.
pleasurable.clue: The warm breeze on the balcony was pleasurable, and nobody wanted to go back inside.

plethora.meaning: If there is a plethora of something, there is far more of it than anyone could ever use.
plethora.clue: The school library has a plethora of books about space but hardly any about castles.

plight.meaning: Someone in a plight is stuck in a situation that is miserable and very hard to escape.
plight.clue: The librarian described the plight of families who had nowhere warm to sleep that winter.

plume.meaning: When smoke curls upwards from a fire or an engine, that twisting column of grey is called a plume.
plume.clue: A white plume of steam rose above the railway arch as the express train thundered past below.

plummet.meaning: To plummet is to fall head first through the air, dropping further and further in no time at all.
plummet.clue: The roller coaster car plummeted from the top of the track, screaming all the way to the bottom.

plump.meaning: Something plump has a soft, rounded shape, like a well-filled cushion or a healthy bird.
plump.clue: A plump robin sat on the fence, puffed up against the freezing morning wind.

plunge.meaning: To plunge into water is to jump in quickly, and the water closes over your head.
plunge.clue: He plunged into the swimming pool to cool down after the cross-country run in the hot sun.

poignant.meaning: Something poignant touches a tender spot in you, so you feel both sadness and a lot of love.
poignant.clue: The old photograph of the school's first teachers was poignant, and several pupils fell silent.

pomposity.meaning: Pomposity is the sound of somebody who talks about themselves in grand, puffed-up words.
pomposity.clue: Local newspapers mocked the pomposity of the speech, which took nearly an hour to say almost nothing.
