ponder.meaning: To ponder a question is to think it over in your head, turning it over and over again.
ponder.clue: We pondered the question of where to go for our trip for nearly an hour.

ponderous.meaning: Something ponderous moves or talks at a slow, heavy pace that makes people lose interest quickly.
ponderous.clue: The ponderous old clock in the hall ticked so slowly that we all fell asleep waiting.

populated.meaning: A populated place is one that plenty of people live in or visit, rather than standing empty.
populated.clue: Once a small fishing village, the cove is now populated mostly by tourists in the summer months.

portal.meaning: A portal is a grand arched entrance through which you step from the street into a building.
portal.clue: We walked through the great stone portal of the castle into the cold, echoing hall.

portentous.meaning: A portentous moment feels heavy with the idea that something important or bad is about to happen.
portentous.clue: There was a portentous silence in the hall as the headteacher read out the exam results.

portrayal.meaning: A portrayal is the way an actor shows a character, using voice, face and movement.
portrayal.clue: Her portrayal of the wicked witch in the school play frightened the whole audience.

poultry.meaning: Chickens, ducks and turkeys kept on a farm for their meat and their eggs.
poultry.clue: At the farmers' market, Dad bought a whole roast chicken and a dozen free-range eggs.

practical.meaning: A plan is practical when it can really be done and put to use.
practical.clue: We had to find a practical way to get forty costumes ready for Friday's play.

pragmatic.meaning: Someone is pragmatic when they care more about solving the problem than about being perfect.
pragmatic.clue: The head teacher took a pragmatic approach, keeping the concert indoors because the rain would not stop.

precedent.meaning: Once a school has set a precedent, later decisions can follow the same pattern.
precedent.clue: Our head teacher set a precedent by letting pupils eat lunch outside all week.

precipitate.meaning: A single noise can precipitate a whole crowd's reaction within seconds.
precipitate.clue: A sudden loud bang precipitated a panic among the Year 6 team waiting by the gate.

precipitous.meaning: A precipitous slope rises or falls so sharply that climbing it is dangerous.
precipitous.clue: The mountain path was so precipitous that we tied the younger children to a rope.

preclude.meaning: Heavy rain can preclude a match, meaning that the game simply cannot take place.
preclude.clue: Bad weather precluded us from holding the picnic, so the class ate in the hall.

precocious.meaning: A precocious pupil asks questions and takes on duties way beyond her years.
precocious.clue: Maya read books written for secondary school pupils, which made her seem remarkably grown-up for her age.

predator.meaning: Every animal is either a predator or the food that a predator hunts.
predator.clue: The owl is a nighttime predator, hunting small mice across the fields.

predecessor.meaning: A new head teacher takes the place of a predecessor who has already left the school.
predecessor.clue: The new computer is much faster than its predecessor, which we used for assemblies.

predilection.meaning: If someone has a predilection for something, they choose it again and again.
predilection.clue: Marta's love of poetry was so strong that she read nothing else, and her teacher set up a poetry club.

predominantly.meaning: When a crowd is made up almost entirely of one sort of person, we say it is predominantly that kind of crowd.
predominantly.clue: The audience was predominantly made up of Year 6 pupils and their families.

prelude.meaning: The drum solo was only a prelude to the huge parade that followed it.
prelude.clue: A short trumpet fanfare acted as a prelude to the school's annual sports day.

preposterous.meaning: An excuse that is plainly untrue sounds preposterous to everyone who hears it.
preposterous.clue: Nobody believed the new boy's tale of fighting off six burglars single-handed with a cricket bat.

prestige.meaning: A school gains prestige when it produces work that other schools admire.
prestige.clue: Winning the national art competition was the highlight of the year and won our school great respect.

presumptuous.meaning: It is presumptuous to invite yourself to a party without being asked.
presumptuous.clue: Sam walked into the head teacher's office, moved her papers and ordered us to wait outside.

prevail.meaning: When one side prevails, it is the side that finally wins the argument.
prevail.clue: In the end common sense prevailed, and the class agreed to put the bins in the right place.

prim.meaning: Someone with a prim manner never relaxes and worries about saying the wrong thing.
prim.clue: My grandmother is so old-fashioned that she will not sit on the sofa or wear jeans in the house.

prioritise.meaning: With many jobs to do, you must decide which to prioritise and which can wait.
prioritise.clue: In an emergency, our head teacher decided to get the youngest children out first, as they were the most frightened.

probability.meaning: In maths a probability is the chance of something happening, worked out from the number of possible results.
probability.clue: Our maths set asked how likely each weather forecast was, and the clear blue sky made tomorrow's rain very unlikely.

problematic.meaning: Something becomes problematic when it is awkward to manage and causes further trouble.
problematic.clue: Rearranging the whole library in one afternoon was a bad plan, since half the classes needed the corridor.

proclivity.meaning: A proclivity for a game, a food or a bad habit is a strong pull towards it.
proclivity.clue: Every time we play chess, Sam cheats at the first sign of losing, which is a habit we are trying to break.

procure.meaning: To procure a piece of equipment means going out of your way to get hold of one.
procure.clue: Through a fund from local businesses, our school was able to buy a brand-new oven for the food room.

prodigal.meaning: A prodigal spender wastes money that ought to have been saved or spent better.
prodigal.clue: The head boy had spent the charity money on trainers for his team, and everyone thought him very careless.

prodigious.meaning: A prodigious effort means far more work or energy than anybody expected.
prodigious.clue: Nobody expected the choir to sing with such vast energy, filling the whole hall in under five minutes.

prodigy.meaning: A musical prodigy may play better than her own teacher at the age of eight.
prodigy.clue: Although she is only eleven, Amira's playing at the concert was astonishing for someone so young.

profane.meaning: It is profane to laugh, swear or eat carelessly while other people are praying.
profane.clue: Someone laughed and ate crisps during the prayers in the mosque, and the guide looked shocked and disappointed.

profess.meaning: To profess an opinion is to announce it openly as something you truly believe.
profess.clue: He insisted with great confidence that he knew nothing about the broken window, but his coat was covered in glass.

proficient.meaning: After enough practice a beginner can become proficient and be trusted to work alone.
proficient.clue: After only a few weeks, Ben could play the saxophone well enough to join the school band.

profit.meaning: A shop makes a profit when what it sells brings in more money than it spends.
profit.clue: At the end of the year the head boy showed that the school shop had made thirty pounds, which was spent on books.

profound.meaning: A profound idea goes far beneath the surface, while a trivial one is worth very little.
profound.clue: The change was profound: within a year, the club had grown from three members to three hundred.

profusion.meaning: The orchard gave such a profusion of apples that we were still eating them in November.
profusion.clue: In summer the garden gives away armfuls of roses, and passers-by stop to take some home.

proliferation.meaning: The proliferation of a plant or a rule means that its numbers keep rising.
proliferation.clue: There are now so many bicycles in the sheds that the school has had to build a second rack.

prolific.meaning: A prolific author writes book after book, whereas a barren year brings nothing at all.
prolific.clue: The apple tree in the playground produced so many apples this year that we could not pick them all.

prologue.meaning: A prologue often hints at events that the main part of the story will explain.
prologue.clue: At the start of the book, the author describes a storm destroying the town, which explains the whole story.

prominent.meaning: A prominent person is one that everybody in a place knows about.
prominent.clue: Mr Patel is a leading figure at school, and his name always appears first on the newsletter.

promote.meaning: Good reviews promote a book, and a strong team promotes its school.
promote.clue: The new scheme gives free tickets to every class, to help more pupils choose science at GCSE.

prompt.meaning: A prompt reply arrives straight away rather than days later.
prompt.clue: One whistle from the coach was enough, and the team was on the pitch in seconds.

pronounce.meaning: Letters such as w and v are hard for a child to pronounce until she learns to use them.
pronounce.clue: Our Welsh guide struggled to say the name of her village clearly, practising it under her breath.

prophetic.meaning: A prophetic warning comes true, and we can only admire it when we look back.
prophetic.clue: Two days before the roof leaked, Daniel had told us exactly that would happen, and nobody believed him.

proportion.meaning: A large proportion of the class means most of it rather than a small part.
proportion.clue: Nearly half the class came back from the trip completely exhausted, which surprised everyone.

propriety.meaning: In a formal room propriety demands that you do not speak while others are speaking.
propriety.clue: When the head teacher came into the dining hall, everyone sat down quietly at once.

prospective.meaning: A prospective prefect is a pupil who has been chosen and will take the job.
prospective.clue: Anyone hoping to become a prefect must attend the training session in the library next Tuesday.

prosper.meaning: A business prospers when more and more customers come to it over the years.
prosper.clue: After the new road opened, the village shop became so busy that they had to hire two more staff.

prosperous.meaning: A prosperous area has good houses, busy shops and work for the people who live there.
prosperous.clue: The little fishing village has more cars and bigger houses than it did ten years ago, thanks to the summer tourists.

protagonist.meaning: The protagonist changes over the course of a story, and the ending shows what they have learnt.
protagonist.clue: The main figure in the story is a shy girl who trains hard and goes on to win the county final.

protract.meaning: Wet weather protracted our journey, so we reached the hills long after dark.
protract.clue: A broken radiator meant the staff meeting stayed in the hall for three hours instead of one.

proverb.meaning: A proverb is easy to remember, so generations of teachers can use the very same few words.
proverb.clue: Grandad would always end his advice with a short saying, and we were meant to work out what it meant.

provincial.meaning: Provincial towns often have one shop of each kind instead of several, and very little choice.
provincial.clue: Our town has one set of traffic lights, a butcher's shop and no cinema at all, yet everybody seems content.

provisional.meaning: A provisional result may be changed later, so it is not safe to celebrate yet.
provisional.clue: The council's approval for our school trip is only in place for now, and they may change their minds later.

provocative.meaning: Provocative behaviour is done on purpose, to stir people up or to get everybody looking.
provocative.clue: His provocative comment about the new library rules made everyone at lunch argue for the rest of the day.

proximity.meaning: Words such as nearby and next door show proximity between two places.
proximity.clue: The proximity of the exam hall to our classroom means we can walk there in a minute.

prudence.meaning: If you show prudence, you think things through before you act, so nobody gets hurt.
prudence.clue: It was the prudence of the trip leader to check the forecast before we set off.

pugnacious.meaning: A pugnacious pupil is the one who cannot walk past an argument without joining it.
pugnacious.clue: Our new class monitor is a bit pugnacious, so she has had two rows with the others.

pulverise.meaning: Anything broken down that finely can no longer be picked out or handled, however big it began.
pulverise.clue: The old brick wall was pulverised so quickly that the workers turned it into a soft grey powder.

punitive.meaning: Deterring others matters more than the fairness of the punishment, in this view.
punitive.clue: The head teacher thought a whole week of extra homework was too punitive for one missed lesson.

quagmire.meaning: Wellington boots are essential when a country path has turned to mud several inches deep.
quagmire.clue: After two days of rain, the path across the playing field became a quagmire of mud and puddles.

quarantine.meaning: Nobody was allowed in or out of the farm for weeks because of disease among the animals.
quarantine.clue: The whole poultry shed was put in quarantine for a fortnight to stop the flu going round.

quarry.meaning: Cranes and lorries haul the blocks away, and the hollow left behind slowly fills with water.
quarry.clue: Our geography trip ended at a huge quarry where a lorry dropped a block the size of our car.

queer.meaning: Something queer is so far from the usual that people stop and stare at it.
queer.clue: We heard a queer noise behind the sports hall and found a fox stuck under the bike shed.

quell.meaning: The head teacher quelled the hubbub in the corridor by standing still and waiting.
quell.clue: One confident sixth former managed to quell the panic when the alarm rang during assembly.

querulous.meaning: Some people are always querulous, objecting to whatever the family decides to do.
querulous.clue: Our new neighbour became quite querulous when the bin men would not empty the back garden on time.

quintessential.meaning: To call somebody quintessential is to say they show that quality more than anyone else.
quintessential.clue: With her muddy boots and endless questions about pond life, she is the quintessential school naturalist.

quip.meaning: Humour of this kind needs only one sentence, because a quip is always short and sharp.
quip.clue: My uncle always answers with a quip when somebody asks him how he is today.

quixotic.meaning: Such plans sound noble and thrilling, but the dreamer rarely gets anywhere with them.
quixotic.clue: His quixotic plan to sail round the world in a small boat will probably fail.

quizzical.meaning: The sign of it is a half smile and one raised eyebrow, saying I do not quite believe you.
quizzical.clue: She gave me a quizzical look when I said that I had brought my own pencil case.

ramification.meaning: It is the knock-on effects, not the first result, that this word is used for.
ramification.clue: The main ramification of closing the corner shop was that we now walk a mile for milk.

ramshackle.meaning: Such a building creaks in the wind, with loose boards and a roof that leaks.
ramshackle.clue: We were shown a ramshackle shed at the far end of the garden to keep our bikes in.

rancour.meaning: Grudges can survive for years in families, and that long-lasting bitterness is called rancour.
rancour.clue: Years of rancour between the two families were finally ended when the old wall came down.

rank.meaning: Rank also means to arrange people in order from the highest down to the lowest.
rank.clue: A high rank in the school choir means you sit at the front of the stage.

ransack.meaning: Someone who ransacks a handbag is hunting for one small lost item and turning out every pocket.
ransack.clue: She had to ransack her school bag in the corridor to find her library book.

rant.meaning: A person who rants will not be quiet until everybody nearby has heard their complaints.
rant.clue: The head teacher began to rant about the state of the changing rooms after the match.

rapacious.meaning: Such a person is never satisfied, however much money and property they have already gathered.
rapacious.clue: The rapacious developers bought up every shop on the high street and put up flats.

rare.meaning: A blue lorry is a rare sight, so drivers slow down to stare at it.
rare.clue: It is rare for our school to win the athletics cup, but we did it twice last year.

rarity.meaning: A thing has rarity when it is so seldom found that owning one is a special event.
rarity.clue: The rarity of a total eclipse of the sun made people travel from many countries to see it.

ratify.meaning: Until the document is signed by everybody, the decision has no force in law.
ratify.clue: Both schools had to ratify the plan to share a coach for the athletics trip.

rationale.meaning: When a head explains a new rule, the account of the thinking behind it is the rationale.
rationale.clue: The pupils asked for the rationale behind banning mobile phones from the playground.

reactionary.meaning: Such people are often afraid that new ideas will take away what they are used to.
reactionary.clue: Some members were so reactionary that they voted against the new computers in the library.

reap.meaning: The same word is used for ripe fields in autumn and for prizes won after long work.
reap.clue: The farmer said we could reap the apples ourselves if we picked them carefully.

recalcitrant.meaning: Such pupils can stop a whole class, because nobody else will start the work.
recalcitrant.clue: The recalcitrant boys in year nine would not line up when the bell rang.

recant.meaning: Doing that can be the bravest thing a witness does in a court of law.
recant.clue: In court the witness chose to recant his statement after seeing the new evidence.

recede.meaning: A receding tide shows the sea going further out and leaving more beach uncovered.
recede.clue: The flood water began to recede on Tuesday, so our street was passable again at last.

receive.meaning: Receiving can be a happy thing, as with a present, or just a fact, as with a letter.
receive.clue: Every pupil who enters the writing competition will receive a certificate at the end of term.

receptacle.meaning: Ask a pupil to name ten receptacles in this classroom and the list will fill a page.
receptacle.clue: We used a tall glass receptacle to keep the pencils upright on the desk.

receptive.meaning: A receptive audience listens closely and is ready to be convinced by a good argument.
receptive.clue: Our form teacher is receptive to ideas, so she let the class plan its own charity day.

recite.meaning: The speaker has to trust their memory alone, because no paper is ever held up.
recite.clue: At the end of assembly, two pupils recited a poem about their first day at school.

recluse.meaning: The old man in the top-floor flat seemed happy to be a recluse, with no visitors at all.
recluse.clue: The recluse in the old mill house never spoke to anybody, and the children only saw him at the shop.

recollection.meaning: Ask an old grandparent for a recollection of their first day at school and listen closely.
recollection.clue: Her first recollection of school was of hiding behind the door on her very first morning.

recompense.meaning: A cheque for lost wages is a recompense for the time and trouble that was caused.
recompense.clue: The council gave a small recompense to the man whose shed the wall had fallen on.

reconcile.meaning: When two people who have fallen out become friendly once more, they have been reconciled.
reconcile.clue: A shared apology from the caretaker helped reconcile the two boys after their argument.

recondite.meaning: Such writing suits an expert, but leaves an eleven-year-old completely lost.
recondite.clue: The instructions for the new science club were so recondite that nobody understood them.

recount.meaning: It is the step by step telling of events that this word is used for.
recount.clue: In assembly, the police officer recounted how he had found the lost dog near the river.

recycle.meaning: Plastic tubs come back as new products rather than ending up on a rubbish tip.
recycle.clue: Our class started a scheme to recycle empty bottles and raised over fifty pounds for charity.

redolent.meaning: Certain scents unlock memories, so that a whiff of perfume brings back a whole afternoon.
redolent.clue: The kitchen was redolent of baking cakes, which made the whole class feel hungry.

redress.meaning: Redressing an injustice may mean saying sorry, paying money back, or changing a rule.
redress.clue: The head teacher tried to redress the wrong by writing to every parent about the mix-up.

redundant.meaning: Redundancy happens when a thing or a person is simply not needed to do a job any more.
redundant.clue: Our old laptops became redundant when the school bought a brand new set for the classroom.

reel.meaning: Dizzy spells, sudden shocks and fast fairground rides can all make a body do this.
reel.clue: He reeled when the spinning ride stopped suddenly and had to sit down on the wall.

reflective.meaning: A reflective pupil sits quietly working out why an answer went wrong.
reflective.clue: After the match, the captain was reflective about the goals he had missed.

reformation.meaning: Existing parts are kept but rearranged and improved, rather than thrown away entirely.
reformation.clue: The reformation of the school timetable has brought us far more time for our library lessons.

refuse.meaning: An honest no is better than agreeing and then failing to turn up.
refuse.clue: She had to refuse the invitation to the party since she was going away that weekend.

regime.meaning: The name given to the rulers who run a country, often with the idea that ordinary people have little power.
regime.clue: Ordinary families lived in constant fear, because those strict rulers controlled every part of their daily lives.

regretful.meaning: Full of sorry thoughts about a past mistake, and wishing you had acted differently.
regretful.clue: He looked down at the floor, regretful that he had shouted at his little sister.

regulate.meaning: When a school or a government sets the limits, it is laying down rules that everybody must stick to.
regulate.clue: The head teacher set strict limits on when and how pupils might use their mobile phones.

reimburse.meaning: An organisation that gives you back what you spent is paying your expenses back to you.
reimburse.clue: After our coach broke down, the school gave my mother her money back for the wasted journey.

reinvigorate.meaning: A good night's sleep or a short holiday can leave you feeling energetic and ready to start again.
reinvigorate.clue: After a short sleep in the car, the two players felt full of energy for the second half of the match.

reiterate.meaning: Saying a warning or a point a second time, firmly, so that nobody can say they did not hear it.
reiterate.clue: The head teacher said the same warning again, because three pupils had still not understood the rule.

rejuvenate.meaning: Making something tired or old-feeling look and feel young and fresh once more.
rejuvenate.clue: A week at the seaside with Grandad worked wonders, and she came home looking years younger.

relay.meaning: Handing news on to the next person in the chain, so that it reaches everybody.
relay.clue: When the bell rang, the pupil at the back shouted the message across the playground to the others.

release.meaning: Opening a cage, ending a hold on something, or putting a new product into the shops.
release.clue: The keeper opened the gate and let the rescued otter go back into the water at last.

relegate.meaning: Sending a team or a person down the table because they performed worse than the others.
relegate.clue: After the season ended, the goalkeeper was moved down to the bench because he had not played.

relentless.meaning: Pressure that never lets up and wears the people who have to keep going.
relentless.clue: The rain fell without a break all afternoon, so the players stood shivering beside the touchline for hours.

relinquish.meaning: Giving up a possession, a right or a duty, when nobody was forcing you to let it go.
relinquish.clue: At the end of the match the captain gave up his place in the team so the injured goalkeeper could play.

reluctant.meaning: Doing something you would rather avoid, and only going along with it because there is no real choice.
reluctant.clue: She said yes, but her trembling hands showed that she would rather have stayed in her seat.

remainder.meaning: In a maths puzzle, the amount you still have to work out after the other shares have been subtracted.
remainder.clue: After paying the deposit, the rest of the trip cost was paid in two equal instalments.

remedy.meaning: Something you try that makes a bad situation or a complaint less bad than it was.
remedy.clue: My grandmother always said that hot soup, early nights and thick scarves were the best answer to a winter cough.

reminiscent.meaning: A smell, a tune or a view that carries you straight back to an earlier time in your life.
reminiscent.clue: The smell of chalk dust in the new hall was strikingly familiar, like an old classroom from childhood.

remnant.meaning: What survives of something bigger after most of it has been eaten, used or broken.
remnant.clue: Only a few crumbs of the enormous cake were left on the plate after the party.

remorse.meaning: The heavy feeling you get inside when you know that you have hurt somebody badly.
remorse.clue: He could not sleep for days, and the awful feeling in his chest would not let him forget what he had done.

remunerate.meaning: Paying a helper or a worker, so that the effort they put in is recognised in money.
remunerate.clue: The council agreed to give every helper who had given up their free time some money for guiding the runners.

rendition.meaning: One particular reading of a piece, which sounds different every time a different person performs it.
rendition.clue: When she sang the school song at the concert, even the visiting parents were moved to clap.

renegade.meaning: A soldier or leader who sells his loyalty to the other side and expects a reward for it.
renegade.clue: During the war, the soldier who slipped away to join the enemy was despised by the men he had abandoned.

renewable.meaning: Able to be used again and again, because nature keeps making more of it.
renewable.clue: Wind and water power are cheap because neither of them ever runs out, unlike coal or oil.

renounce.meaning: Promising in public to give something up for good, and never to claim it again.
renounce.clue: In his speech, the old king turned his back on the treaty and refused to accept any part of it.

repel.meaning: Sending a person, an animal or an attack packing, usually because it comes at you unpleasantly.
repel.clue: The cold wind at the top of the hill was enough to send the tired walkers back down again.

repercussions.meaning: The knock-on effects that follow a decision, long after it has been made.
repercussions.clue: The argument over the new school rule had serious knock-on effects, and three families soon moved away.

replica.meaning: A duplicate so exact that visitors cannot tell it apart from the thing it was copied from.
replica.clue: Visitors queued to walk through the huge model of the cathedral, which looked exactly like the real building.

reprehensible.meaning: The sort of conduct that makes an ordinary decent person shake their head in disgust.
reprehensible.clue: The head teacher said that copying another pupil's work was dishonest and morally wrong.

repress.meaning: Turning a feeling inwards and keeping it hidden, so that nobody around you realises.
repress.clue: He struggled to keep a straight face during the boring talk, but his red ears gave him away.

reprieve.meaning: Extra time granted to somebody who was facing punishment, with the threat still hanging over them.
reprieve.clue: Because she had helped the police, the judge let the young thief off with only a warning for now.

reproach.meaning: Telling someone firmly that you are disappointed with what they have done.
reproach.clue: The class teacher looked at the boy in front of the whole class and told him she was disappointed.

reprove.meaning: A firm telling-off in words, given because an adult is not prepared to let something pass.
reprove.clue: The head teacher told the boys firmly that running noisily down the corridor during registration was unacceptable.

repudiate.meaning: Turning your back on something you were once ready to believe, and saying so in public.
repudiate.clue: The charity dismissed the newspaper's accusation as untrue and demanded a written apology from the writer.

repugnant.meaning: The kind of smell, sight or behaviour that makes you turn your head away on the spot.
repugnant.clue: The smell of the overflowing bins at the back of the kitchen made several pupils hold their noses.

reputation.meaning: What people say about you when you are not in the room.
reputation.clue: Years of fair play and shaking hands with the other side gave the captain a name for good sportsmanship.

rescind.meaning: Undoing an official decision, as if it had never been agreed in the first place.
rescind.clue: Because the lunch box rule had caused so much trouble, the governors decided at the last meeting that it should no longer exist.

reserve.meaning: Putting a seat, a slice or a whole afternoon to one side so that it is still there when you need it.
reserve.clue: She asked the waiter to hold the table by the window, because her friends were late again.

reside.meaning: Where a person makes their permanent base, whether that is a flat, a village or a town.
reside.clue: Every house in our road was built in the 1920s, and the same families have been here for decades.

residence.meaning: The building a person actually sleeps and lives in, as opposed to the place they work in.
residence.clue: The prime minister's official London address is well known, and photographers often crowd outside the gates.

residue.meaning: Just a trace left behind, not enough to be of much use to anybody.
residue.clue: After the fire, only a thin layer of grey ash was still on the floor of the shed.

resign.meaning: Handing in your notice and leaving a job for good, without being forced out.
resign.clue: After ten years as a caretaker, Mr Ali handed in his notice because he wanted a quieter life.

resilience.meaning: Bouncing back after a setback, like getting up and trying again after a bad day.
resilience.clue: What the pupil showed after losing the final was remarkable: she trained twice as hard the next morning.

resist.meaning: Standing your ground when somebody pushes, begs or threatens you to change your mind.
resist.clue: She could not stand the pressure from her friends, so she refused to change her answer.

resort.meaning: Families book a room there in the summer because the weather is warm and there is plenty for children to do.
resort.clue: Our class stayed at a small holiday park near the beach, and the queue for swimming pools started before breakfast.

respite.meaning: A welcome pause in the middle of something hard, when nobody is asking anything of you.
respite.clue: After the storm the fishermen waited a whole week for calm weather before going out again.

resplendent.meaning: Such brilliance and beauty that the whole room seems to light up when you walk in.
resplendent.clue: The bride's dress was covered in silver sparkles, and everyone turned to look as she walked down the aisle.

responsibility.meaning: It is your duty to look after something and to answer for what happens to it.
responsibility.clue: It was hers to lock up the classroom at four, so she checked the door twice before going home.

restless.meaning: Constant wriggling, shifting and complaining, because something inside will not settle.
restless.clue: By lunchtime the class was tapping, chatting and swinging on their chairs, waiting for the bell.

restore.meaning: Bringing a damaged building, picture or old custom back to the condition it was in before.
restore.clue: The old bicycle shed was fixed last spring, and now the pupils lock their bikes there safely again.

restraint.meaning: Choosing not to act on a sudden urge, even though every finger itches to do it.
restraint.clue: He wanted to shout at the referee, but good sense and calm kept the words inside his mouth.

retain.meaning: Still having something afterwards, instead of giving it away or losing it.
retain.clue: Even after she moved away, she still had the letter that her grandmother had written to her.

retaliate.meaning: If you retaliate, you answer harm done to you with harm of your own.
retaliate.clue: After Finn deliberately knocked his books over, Callum decided to retaliate by spreading an embarrassing rumour.

reticent.meaning: A reticent person keeps their thoughts to themselves and finds it hard to speak openly.
reticent.clue: At the parents' evening, Aisha was so reticent that her teacher had to draw every detail out of her.

retiring.meaning: Someone who is retiring avoids drawing attention to themselves in a group.
retiring.clue: Chloe was so retiring in her new class that she never raised her hand, even when she knew the answer.

retort.meaning: A retort is a reply you make at once, usually a bit sharp, when someone says something to you.
retort.clue: When Tom said the results were rigged, Priya retorted that she had watched him copying half the answers.

retract.meaning: To retract something you said means to take it back and admit that you were wrong.
retract.clue: The newspaper had to retract its claim about the new stadium once it discovered the photograph showed a different building.

retrieve.meaning: If you retrieve something, you go and get it, usually because it has been lost or put away.
retrieve.clue: Danny retrieved his football boots from the shed just before the match and kicked a hat-trick.

reveal.meaning: Revealing a secret means telling other people something that was being kept hidden.
reveal.clue: The sealed envelope revealed the names of the pupils who had won a place at the grammar school.

reverence.meaning: Reverence is the very great respect you feel for a person or thing you consider holy or admirable.
reverence.clue: The old cathedral was treated with great reverence, and nobody walked across its yard while the service was taking place.

revile.meaning: To revile someone is to attack them with words full of hatred and disgust.
revile.clue: In her speech, the candidate reviled opponents who wanted the old town hall demolished, calling them vandals.

revive.meaning: Reviving something means bringing it back to life or making people feel interested in it again.
revive.clue: Volunteers revived interest in the crumbling swimming pool by clearing it and holding a fundraiser.

revolutionise.meaning: When something is revolutionised, it changes so completely that life afterwards is quite different.
revolutionise.clue: The invention of the washing machine revolutionised homes, saving families hours of scrubbing every week.

rhapsody.meaning: A rhapsody is a long, free-flowing piece of music that expresses a whole mood or story.
rhapsody.clue: The orchestra played a rhapsody at the concert, and the audience sat completely silent throughout.

rhetoric.meaning: Rhetoric is grand, impressive talk used to win people over rather than to explain things clearly.
rhetoric.clue: His speech was full of fine rhetoric, but the audience soon noticed he had offered no real answer to their questions.

ridicule.meaning: To ridicule a person is to make fun of them, usually in front of other people.
ridicule.clue: Because he pronounced his own name wrongly, the class began to ridicule him and he refused to speak for a week.

righteous.meaning: Being righteous means being so good and blameless that others hold you up as an example.
righteous.clue: In the story, the righteous villager is rewarded for telling the truth even though he loses his job.

rivalry.meaning: Rivalry means the fierce or friendly competition that grows up between two rivals.
rivalry.clue: The rivalry between the two schools has grown since their teams met in the final and won by one point.

robust.meaning: Something that is robust is solidly built and will not easily be broken by bumps or bad weather.
robust.clue: These robust boots were designed for hill walking, so they should survive months of mud and rain.

rogue.meaning: A rogue is someone dishonest or mischievous who does not behave the way a decent person should.
rogue.clue: A rogue trading-card dealer sold fake cards to children, and the shop refused to give the money back.

rueful.meaning: If you look rueful, you show that you are sorry about what has happened and slightly embarrassed by it.
rueful.clue: He looked rueful when he realised he had eaten the last of his mother's birthday cake.

rummage.meaning: To rummage means to dig through untidy piles of things, looking for what you want.
rummage.clue: Mum had to rummage through every drawer in the kitchen before she found the tin opener.

ruthless.meaning: Someone who is ruthless shows no mercy at all, even towards people who are helpless.
ruthless.clue: The ruthless captain dropped the youngest boy from the team after a single mistake.

sabotage.meaning: To sabotage something means to damage it or spoil its plans deliberately, usually in secret.
sabotage.clue: Someone had tried to sabotage the school's charity bake sale, but a pupil spotted the hidden note.

sacred.meaning: Something sacred is holy and set apart, so it is treated with deep respect and never used casually.
sacred.clue: The ancient stones were considered sacred, which is why visitors must never climb or carve on them.

sanctimonious.meaning: Someone who is sanctimonious pretends to be deeply good in a way that makes other people uncomfortable.
sanctimonious.clue: He was always sanctimonious about helping at the food bank, yet he never actually turned up.

sanctity.meaning: The sanctity of a place or tradition means that it is holy and deserves to be treated with great care.
sanctity.clue: Visitors were asked to respect the sanctity of the church by keeping their voices low and taking off their shoes.

sanctuary.meaning: A sanctuary is a safe place where nobody will hurt you or ask awkward questions.
sanctuary.clue: The old chapel was used as a sanctuary for those who had nowhere else to sleep that winter.

sane.meaning: Someone who is sane thinks clearly and behaves reasonably rather than in a wild or confused way.
sane.clue: Her answers in the mock interview sounded so sane that the panel began to trust her judgement completely.

sarcastic.meaning: A sarcastic remark says one thing but means something quite different, usually something unkind.
sarcastic.clue: His comment that the new kit was fashionable was sarcastic, since the whole team actually hated it.

satin.meaning: Satin is a thin material with a smooth, shiny surface that catches the light.
satin.clue: The bride's dress was made of satin, and it swished beautifully as she walked to the front.

satisfying.meaning: Something satisfying makes you feel pleased because it gives you a real sense of achievement.
satisfying.clue: Painting the whole fence was hard work, but the neighbours said the result was deeply satisfying.

savour.meaning: To savour something means to enjoy it slowly, paying attention to how it tastes or smells.
savour.clue: We sat outside on the step savouring the hot soup and pretending that the rain might stop.

savoury.meaning: Food that is savoury has a salty, herby or peppery taste rather than a sweet one.
savoury.clue: The stall sold only savoury snacks, so we bought cheese pastries instead of doughnuts for the journey home.

scarcity.meaning: Scarcity means that there is very little of something, so people have to manage without it.
scarcity.clue: Because of the scarcity of clean water, each family was given two bottles a day.

scathing.meaning: A scathing remark criticises something harshly and in great detail.
scathing.clue: The review was scathing, pointing out every fault in the film without a single word of praise.

scenic.meaning: A scenic route or area is one you visit for the beautiful views, not for convenience.
scenic.clue: We took the scenic route over the hills because the coach drivers said the view was wonderful.

sceptical.meaning: To be sceptical about something means to doubt it and to expect it to be false or disappointing.
sceptical.clue: Priya was sceptical about the free lunch offer and insisted on checking the small print first.

scholastic.meaning: A scholastic achievement is one connected with schoolwork, study or formal education.
scholastic.clue: Her scholastic record was so strong that two universities wrote to her before she had finished school.

score.meaning: A score is the total number of points a team or player gets in a game or test.
score.clue: Their final score of thirty-four was enough to win by a narrow margin, and the crowd went wild.

scrutinise.meaning: To scrutinise something means to study it very closely, usually looking for mistakes or problems.
scrutinise.clue: The examiner scrutinised every calculation on the page before awarding marks, and two answers were changed.

sculpture.meaning: A sculpture is a work of art that has been shaped out of solid material such as wood, stone or metal.
sculpture.clue: The bronze sculpture in the town square was stolen during the night, leaving only a clean square base.

scurrilous.meaning: Scurrilous language is abusive and insulting, and it can damage a person's good name.
scurrilous.clue: The newspaper printed scurrilous claims about the family that turned out to be completely untrue.

seclusion.meaning: Seclusion means being completely on your own, away from other people and any noise.
seclusion.clue: She loved the seclusion of her grandmother's cottage, with no television and no traffic outside the gate.

secretive.meaning: Someone who is secretive deliberately keeps information to themselves and hides what they are doing.
secretive.clue: Our new pupil was so secretive that none of us could tell where he lived or which club he joined.

sectarian.meaning: Sectarian behaviour means backing one group so strongly that you dismiss everybody else.
sectarian.clue: The discussion turned sectarian when two pupils began arguing about which religion was the only correct one.

secure.meaning: If something is secure, it is safe and cannot be moved, lost or damaged by accident.
secure.clue: The pupils checked that every window was secure before the storm arrived in the evening.

segment.meaning: A segment is a single part of a bigger whole, like one slice cut from a melon.
segment.clue: She cut the melon into segments and passed them round with a spoon each.

seldom.meaning: Seldom means that something happens only a few times and almost never.
seldom.clue: He seldom eats breakfast, and by first break he is already hungry and out of temper.

self-righteous.meaning: A self-righteous person believes their own opinions are right and looks down on everyone who differs.
self-righteous.clue: He was self-righteous about recycling, criticising his own family for throwing away a plastic bottle.

semantics.meaning: Semantics is the branch of language study that deals with what words actually mean.
semantics.clue: In his essay on semantics, the pupil argued that an advertisement changes the meaning of ordinary words.

serendipity.meaning: A serendipity is a lucky discovery that nobody planned and nobody was looking for.
serendipity.clue: Finding her grandmother's letters while looking for a blank notebook was pure serendipity and led to a history project.

serenity.meaning: Feeling deeply relaxed and unhurried, with no worries at all.
serenity.clue: On the quiet beach at dawn, she felt a deep serenity that no school bell could ever break.

shrink.meaning: Losing size, quite often because of heat or cold.
shrink.clue: Hot water can make rubber shrink, which is why my new boots felt tight that morning.

significant.meaning: Great enough to be worth mentioning or worth counting.
significant.clue: There was a significant improvement in her handwriting after just one term of practice.

simulate.meaning: Acting out a pretend version of something so that it looks real.
simulate.clue: In the assembly, six pupils simulate a flock of birds, flapping their arms and calling loudly.

simultaneous.meaning: Sharing the very same moment, with no gap between them.
simultaneous.clue: The two swimming lessons are simultaneous, so the whole year must share the one pool.

singular.meaning: Just one, with no others of its kind beside it.
singular.clue: One bright balloon floated past the gate, a singular sight among the dull grey buildings.

skirmish.meaning: A burst of fighting that ends as quickly as it began.
skirmish.clue: During the game, a small skirmish broke out when the ball was kicked over the fence.

slogan.meaning: A few punchy words a company hopes you will remember.
slogan.clue: The new sports drink's slogan was painted across the bus in huge white letters.

slothful.meaning: Happy to sit on the sofa rather than get on with anything.
slothful.clue: A slothful afternoon in front of the television is my idea of perfect relaxation.

slovenly.meaning: Making a mess of how you look or how you work.
slovenly.clue: His slovenly uniform had a muddy hem, a loose button and ink stains down one sleeve.

sluggish.meaning: Never hurrying, like a pond that barely ripples on a warm day.
sluggish.clue: On the hot afternoon, the team's sluggish pace let the other side run away with the match.

sober.meaning: Cool and unsmiling, as though a grave matter were being discussed.
sober.clue: Despite the funny hat, her sober expression told us that the news was very bad.

sociable.meaning: Someone who mixes easily and enjoys chatting to new people.
sociable.clue: At the party, the sociable girl greeted every guest and introduced them to one another.

solemnity.meaning: A deep, dignified calm that suits an occasion like a funeral.
solemnity.clue: The solemnity of the minute's silence in the hall made everyone lower their voices.

solicit.meaning: Knocking on doors and asking strangers for support or money.
solicit.clue: The charity volunteers went from house to house to solicit donations for the food bank.

solitude.meaning: Peaceful time spent alone with nobody else around.
solitude.clue: She spent the afternoon in solitude, reading on the quiet beach below the dunes.

sophisticated.meaning: Very clever and high-tech, like a machine built by real experts.
sophisticated.clue: The new laboratory uses sophisticated equipment that can test a drop of water in seconds.

specify.meaning: Saying exactly what you mean, leaving no room for guessing.
specify.clue: The coach asked us to specify the exact time of the match, not simply say it was after lunch.

spendthrift.meaning: Someone who cannot stop spending money they ought to save.
spendthrift.clue: Our neighbour is a real spendthrift, and his savings never last beyond the first week.

spiteful.meaning: Saying or doing nasty things simply because you dislike someone.
spiteful.clue: The class ignored her spiteful comments because everyone knew they came from jealousy.

spontaneity.meaning: Doing whatever comes into your head at once, without any plan at all.
spontaneity.clue: The comedian's spontaneity kept the crowd laughing, because he had written no jokes at all.

sporadic.meaning: Turning up by chance, with long gaps in between.
sporadic.clue: Rain fell in sporadic bursts, so the players left the pitch twice and came back soaked.

spurious.meaning: Not true at all, however convincing it sounds at first.
spurious.clue: The rumour turned out to be spurious, and the head teacher apologised to the class.

squalor.meaning: Conditions so dirty and sad that living there becomes a daily struggle.
squalor.clue: Volunteers in old clothes collected rubbish from the flats, where squalor had been left for years.

stability.meaning: A settled state that does not shift or fall apart.
stability.clue: The stability of the old wooden bridge was tested every year, and it never shifted at all.

stagnate.meaning: Standing still instead of moving forward or getting better.
stagnate.clue: Interest in the project began to stagnate, and the class stopped working after the first week.

stalemate.meaning: A position in which everybody is stuck and nobody can succeed.
stalemate.clue: The final round reached a stalemate, and the players agreed to share the trophy at last.

stance.meaning: A particular way of holding your body or of thinking about something.
stance.clue: The photograph caught the guard's stance perfectly, with his feet planted wide apart.

static.meaning: Like a photograph rather than a film, with no action and no change at all.
static.clue: The lecture felt static, and by ten minutes the whole audience had drifted into a doze.

stealthy.meaning: Doing things very quietly so that no one will hear or see you.
stealthy.clue: The stealthy fox crossed the garden at midnight and left not a single footprint behind.

stereotype.meaning: A lazy, unfair picture of a whole group that ignores real differences.
stereotype.clue: It is a stereotype that all teenagers are lazy, and our class proves it wrong each day.

stockpile.meaning: Extra things gathered and kept in case they are needed later.
stockpile.clue: During the storm the town used its stockpile of blankets to keep families warm and dry.

stoic.meaning: Someone who keeps a calm face however uncomfortable the situation.
stoic.clue: He remained stoic when his bike was stolen, and never once mentioned it to his parents.

stolid.meaning: Hard to rouse, like somebody who hardly ever reacts to anything.
stolid.clue: His stolid reply gave nothing away, and the interviewer tried a completely different question.

stretched.meaning: Drawn out to a longer length than it was before.
stretched.clue: A thin sheet of ice was stretched across the pond, and it creaked under every footstep.

strident.meaning: So sharp and forceful that people wince or stop and listen.
strident.clue: With a strident voice, the coach shouted his final instructions across the wind and rain.

stringent.meaning: Very demanding, leaving no room for mistakes or excuses.
stringent.clue: The new guidelines are so stringent that even the smallest mistake will be reported.

strive.meaning: Never giving up on something, however much effort it takes.
strive.clue: The school asks every pupil to strive for kindness, even on the days when they feel tired and cross.

strut.meaning: Walking about as if you are showing off how important you are.
strut.clue: The new pupil strut into the classroom as though he already owned the whole school.

stubborn.meaning: So fixed in your opinion that no argument will move you.
stubborn.clue: My little brother is so stubborn that he still insists on wearing his coat in August.

studious.meaning: Fond of books and homework, and happy to work hard at school.
studious.clue: The studious girl in the corner finishes her homework before anyone has opened a pencil case.

stupendous.meaning: So huge and impressive that it leaves everybody speechless.
stupendous.clue: The choir gave a stupendous performance, and the audience rose to their feet for minutes.

stupidity.meaning: Doing something without thinking, and suffering for it afterwards.
stupidity.clue: It was pure stupidity to leave the gate open, and the dog was out in seconds.

suave.meaning: Cool and quietly confident, the way a star of the 1930s would be.
suave.clue: With a suave smile, the salesman asked whether we had ever considered buying a second car.

subjugate.meaning: Taking control of a weaker place or people against their wishes.
subjugate.clue: The army tried to subjugate the island, but the villagers refused to hand over their homes.

sublime.meaning: Wonderfully beautiful, in a way that makes you feel humble.
sublime.clue: From the clifftop the view was sublime, with golden light spreading across the calm sea below.

submit.meaning: Agreeing to do what someone in charge tells you to do.
submit.clue: The children refused to submit to the new rule, so the head teacher called a meeting.

subsequent.meaning: Happening afterwards, once the thing you have just mentioned is over.
subsequent.clue: In subsequent weeks the homework became harder, and our marks began to improve a little.

subservient.meaning: So eager to please others that you never stand up for yourself.
subservient.clue: The subservient waiter let the rude customer shout, and never once stood up for himself.

subside.meaning: Fading away gradually, until the trouble is finally over.
subside.clue: By six o'clock the storm began to subside, and we could hear birds singing in the apple tree.

substance.meaning: If something has substance, it is real material you can see and touch, not just an idea.
substance.clue: The builder said the wall was made of solid substance, but the hollow blocks crumbled.

substantiate.meaning: To substantiate a claim is to gather facts that show it really is true.
substantiate.clue: The reporter needed evidence to substantiate her story before the newspaper agreed to print it.

subtlety.meaning: A subtlety is a tiny hidden meaning that you only notice if you think carefully about the words.
subtlety.clue: There is a subtlety in her reply that made the whole class think twice about the plan.

subtropical.meaning: Somewhere subtropical is near the equator, so it stays warm and damp without being quite as hot as the jungle.
subtropical.clue: In our geography lesson we learned that the subtropical coast has palms and mild winters.

succinct.meaning: A succinct answer gives the whole message quickly, without extra padding or explanation.
succinct.clue: Miss Reid asked for a succinct answer, so Ravi gave it in a single clear sentence.

suggestible.meaning: Someone suggestible does whatever they are told, rather than thinking for themselves.
suggestible.clue: The sales assistant was so suggestible that she bought a coat she had never wanted.

sundry.meaning: Sundry things are lots of different objects gathered together, with no special pattern to them.
sundry.clue: The charity shop sells sundry goods, from old books to chipped teacups and wooden spoons.

supercilious.meaning: A supercilious person looks down on others and assumes that they are far below them.
supercilious.clue: The new boy was supercilious about his old school, so nobody wanted to talk to him.

superior.meaning: Someone superior has more skill, rank or quality than the people they are compared with.
superior.clue: In the trial, the winning team proved superior, playing far more skilfully than their rivals.

supplicate.meaning: To supplicate is to make a very earnest and humble request to somebody important.
supplicate.clue: The lost hikers supplicated for help, and the coastguard sent a boat at once.

surge.meaning: A surge is a sudden wave of increase, like a rush of water or a jump in prices.
surge.clue: A surge of excitement ran through the hall when the exam results were read out.

surly.meaning: A surly person answers you sharply and seems angry or entirely unwilling to help.
surly.clue: The surly man at the shop door told us to come back tomorrow instead of helping us.

surmount.meaning: To surmount something difficult is to get past it and carry on successfully.
surmount.clue: Our team worked hard to surmount the tricky maths problems and finished with a high score.

surpass.meaning: To surpass a record or a rival means to go further and do better than they ever managed.
surpass.clue: Her time in the relay surpassed every other school record set at the sports day.

surreptitious.meaning: Something surreptitious is done quietly, without anybody else being told about it.
surreptitious.clue: The pupil made a surreptitious copy of the answers while the teacher turned away.

surveillance.meaning: Surveillance means keeping a steady eye on something so that danger or trouble is noticed quickly.
surveillance.clue: CCTV surveillance helped the police trace the bike thief within a couple of hours.

suspect.meaning: If you suspect something, you think it may well be true or wrong, even though you cannot be sure.
suspect.clue: The librarian suspected that someone had taken a book, but she had no proof at all.

suspend.meaning: To suspend something is to stop it for a while, usually because somebody in charge has decided so.
suspend.clue: Bad weather forced the school to suspend all outdoor games until the rain finally stopped.

swallow.meaning: To swallow food or drink is to take it down your throat rather than leaving it in your mouth.
swallow.clue: The baby had to swallow her medicine quickly because it tasted so bitter.

swindled.meaning: To be swindled means to be tricked into handing over money for something you never really wanted.
swindled.clue: The trader swindled the club, selling them fake tickets for a match that was never held.

sycophancy.meaning: Sycophancy is sucking up to somebody by telling them exactly what they want to hear.
sycophancy.clue: Staff at the awards night were accused of sycophancy because they praised every single entry.

tangible.meaning: A tangible thing can be touched, counted or shown with clear evidence rather than merely imagined.
tangible.clue: Our head gave us a tangible reward, a certificate that we really could hold in our hands.

tantamount.meaning: Two things are tantamount when having one means exactly the same as having the other.
tantamount.clue: Giving the class extra homework is tantamount to a punishment, since nobody wanted to stay behind.

tapestry.meaning: A tapestry tells a story in coloured threads, worked into a cloth that can cover a whole wall.
tapestry.clue: The castle guide explained that the ancient threads in the tapestry showed a hunting scene from long ago.

taunt.meaning: A taunt is an unkind remark aimed at making somebody feel small or angry.
taunt.clue: The boys on the terrace taunted the new pupil until she turned away in tears.

taxing.meaning: A taxing job or task needs a lot of your energy and leaves you completely worn out.
taxing.clue: The new timetable is taxing, so our form teacher shortened the last lesson and gave us a break.

techily.meaning: To explain something techily means to use the special words that experts in that field use.
techily.clue: The engineer explained the wiring techily, using words none of us had ever heard before.

tedium.meaning: Tedium is the dragging boredom of doing the same dull thing again and again.
tedium.clue: Three hours of revision in a silent room brought on such tedium that we all fell asleep.

temper.meaning: When someone loses their temper, they shout or lash out instead of staying calm.
temper.clue: My brother lost his temper when his football team lost, and he slammed the door.

temptation.meaning: Temptation is the pull of something attractive that you would be foolish to give in to.
temptation.clue: The smell of fresh chips outside the gate was real temptation after a long cross-country run.

tenant.meaning: A tenant rents their home from the person who owns it and pays money to stay there.
tenant.clue: Our new tenant is a student who has rented the upstairs room for the whole year.

tenet.meaning: A tenet is a belief that somebody holds firmly, rather like a rule they always follow.
tenet.clue: The main tenet of our club is that you should never give up, however badly the match goes.

tentative.meaning: A tentative plan is one you are not sure about yet, so you may still change it.
tentative.clue: We made a tentative arrangement to meet outside the library, in case the hall is booked.

termination.meaning: Termination is the point at which a job, contract or arrangement finally stops.
termination.clue: The termination of our tenancy means we must empty the flat and hand back the keys.

terrestrial.meaning: A terrestrial animal lives on land, and a terrestrial planet is a world much like our own.
terrestrial.clue: We compared images of Mars with our own planet and noted how many terrestrial features they share.

terse.meaning: A terse reply is very short and gives the minimum of information, with nothing more added.
terse.clue: The head gave a terse answer, so we still do not know why the trip was cancelled.

texture.meaning: Texture describes how a surface feels when you touch it, such as the roughness of stone.
texture.clue: The artist chose thick paint to add texture to the flat wall of the hall.

thoughtful.meaning: Being thoughtful means remembering how other people feel and choosing kind words and actions.
thoughtful.clue: It was thoughtful of you to save me a seat, because I had been standing all morning.

thrilled.meaning: If you are thrilled about news, the whole of you lights up with pleasure.
thrilled.clue: We were thrilled when the results arrived early, with two names on the first team.

tirade.meaning: A tirade is a flood of angry complaining words that goes on and on without stopping.
tirade.clue: Our neighbour launched a tirade about dog mess, complaining loudly while we all said nothing.

tolerance.meaning: Tolerance means putting up with people who think, look or behave differently from you.
tolerance.clue: Our class showed real tolerance when a pupil joined wearing a headscarf nobody had seen before.

tractable.meaning: A tractable person or animal is easy to guide and goes along with instructions willingly.
tractable.clue: Our new puppy is far more tractable now, and he walks quietly on his lead.

traitor.meaning: A traitor sells out the people who trusted them, usually in exchange for money or power.
traitor.clue: In the play, a traitor handed the castle gates to the enemy while the king slept.

tranquillity.meaning: Tranquillity means being still and untroubled, with nothing at all worrying you for a while.
tranquillity.clue: We enjoyed the tranquillity of the empty library while the storm raged outside.

transcendent.meaning: Something transcendent is so extraordinary that ordinary words seem far too small to describe it.
transcendent.clue: The singing at the concert was transcendent, and the audience forgot to clap for a while.

transfix.meaning: To be transfixed means to be held motionless by shock, fear or wonder, unable to look away.
transfix.clue: The children were transfixed by the trick with the empty sleeve, which really did hold a rabbit.

transformation.meaning: A transformation changes something so completely that it becomes something different altogether.
transformation.clue: The transformation of the old mill into a science museum took just eighteen months of careful work.

transgress.meaning: To transgress a rule is to do something you have been told must never be done.
transgress.clue: Anyone who transgresses the rules of the match will be shown a yellow card.

transient.meaning: A transient feeling comes and goes very quickly, leaving almost no trace behind it.
transient.clue: The heatwave lasted three days, and the swelter was transient once the clouds rolled in.

transparent.meaning: Something transparent is see-through, and a transparent person never tries to hide their feelings.
transparent.clue: The window at the back of our classroom was transparent, so we watched the rain from indoors.

traverse.meaning: Passing right over or through something, from one side or end to the other.
traverse.clue: The walkers had to traverse the whole of the moor before the weather turned, and their legs ached.

treaty.meaning: A deal signed between states that sets out what each side has promised to do.
treaty.clue: At the museum we learnt how the two countries signed a treaty in 1919, ending years of bitter argument.

trepidation.meaning: A sudden rush of worry that sets your heart racing and your hands trembling.
trepidation.clue: With trepidation, Priya opened the exam results envelope, because she had not revised at all.

triumphant.meaning: Being pleased and proud because you have finally beaten a challenge that was hard.
triumphant.clue: The triumphant captain lifted the silver cup as the whole team shouted with pride.

truculent.meaning: Someone who is truculent is quick to lose their temper and to pick fights.
truculent.clue: A truculent new boy argued with the dinner lady about portion sizes until the head teacher stepped in.

truncate.meaning: Taking the end or the bottom off something, so that what is left is smaller than it was.
truncate.clue: Photographers sometimes truncate a long word so that it fits neatly on the title page.

tumult.meaning: A great roar of noise from a big crowd, such as at a concert or a football match.
tumult.clue: When the whistle blew, a tumult of cheering voices filled the hall and rattled the windows.

turmoil.meaning: A period of wild confusion, when everything seems to go wrong at the same time.
turmoil.clue: With the school closed for a week, the head was in turmoil over where every class should go.

twilight.meaning: The soft pale light in the sky just after the sun has gone down.
twilight.clue: At twilight the sky turned pink and the street lamps flickered on one by one along our road.

tyrant.meaning: A powerful person who treats everyone below them badly and demands total obedience.
tyrant.clue: The tyrant ruled the playground for a term, telling everyone where to stand and what to wear.

ubiquitous.meaning: Something that is ubiquitous seems to be everywhere, like mobile phones in a busy city.
ubiquitous.clue: In our house, sticky notes are ubiquitous, and there is one on almost every door.

ultimatum.meaning: A demand that must be obeyed, because the person making it has the power to punish refusal.
ultimatum.clue: Our club president gave everyone an ultimatum: hand in the money by Friday or the trip is off.

unanimous.meaning: Everyone in the group is in favour, so there is not a single person objecting.
unanimous.clue: When the captain asked who had finished the marathon, every hand went up in a unanimous show of support.

uncaring.meaning: Somebody who is uncaring does not stop to think about whether their actions upset others.
uncaring.clue: It was uncaring of Sam to laugh at Ravi's spelling mistake when the whole class could hear him.

uncouth.meaning: Someone who is uncouth makes a scene and talks in a way that upsets the people around him.
uncouth.clue: His uncouth behaviour at the concert, shouting and stamping his feet, embarrassed the whole school party.

underlying.meaning: The cause of something that lies behind what you can see, and explains it.
underlying.clue: Nobody could work out the underlying problem, until we realised the date on the board was wrong.

undermine.meaning: Working quietly against someone so that their influence or reputation is slowly lost.
undermine.clue: The rumour was designed to undermine our captain before the match, and it made her quiet.

undulate.meaning: Moving gently up and down in a series of smooth curves, rather than staying flat.
undulate.clue: The flag began to undulate above the playground as the wind got up during the sports day.

unforgiving.meaning: Someone who is unforgiving holds a grudge long after the argument has ended.
unforgiving.clue: Our head teacher is not usually unforgiving, but the class was shocked when he took away the phones.

uniformity.meaning: When every part of a place is exactly alike, from the curtains to the coats, there is nothing to notice.
uniformity.clue: The head disliked the uniformity of our three identical kits and said the team needed its own style.

union.meaning: A group of people who combine their strength so that they are treated fairly and look after each other.
union.clue: The pupils' union raised money for new sports equipment and negotiated a better lunch break.

universal.meaning: If something is universal, it is true or useful for everybody, not just for one group.
universal.clue: The rule about no mobile phones in lessons is universal: it applies to every pupil in every year group.

unorthodox.meaning: An unorthodox idea works in a completely different way from the ones people expect.
unorthodox.clue: Their unorthodox method of revising, drawing mind maps in colours, worked better than our dull worksheets.

unprecedented.meaning: If an event is unprecedented, nobody can point to anything like it happening before.
unprecedented.clue: Rain stopped play in the final of the cup, a decision the club called unprecedented in its fifty years.

unpretentious.meaning: Someone who is unpretentious is happy to be themselves and does not show off.
unpretentious.clue: Mrs Ahmed is unpretentious, serving tea in ordinary mugs and praising our work without a fuss.

unrequited.meaning: If your love is unrequited, the person you care about does not care about you in the same way.
unrequited.clue: She wrote a short story about unrequited love, where a girl sends letters that are never read.

unrestricted.meaning: If nothing limits an activity, you may take part in it as often and as much as you like.
unrestricted.clue: Entry to the science club is unrestricted, so any pupil may turn up without asking a teacher first.

unscrupulous.meaning: An unscrupulous person will cheat or lie if it helps them, and feels no guilt about it.
unscrupulous.clue: The unscrupulous seller hid the cracks in the piano, knowing that we would never notice.

untoward.meaning: Something untoward gets in the way of what you had arranged, just when you least expect it.
untoward.clue: The coach was ill before the cup final, which was untoward for the team and their supporters.

unwarranted.meaning: A punishment or a remark is unwarranted when there is no good reason for making it.
unwarranted.clue: The head said the rumour about her was unwarranted and should not be repeated by anybody.

unwitting.meaning: An unwitting remark is made by accident, when the speaker had no idea it would be heard.
unwitting.clue: She made an unwitting remark about someone's accent, not realising the girl was sitting beside her.

unworthy.meaning: If you feel unworthy of something, you think you are not good enough to be given it.
unworthy.clue: The head boy felt unworthy of the award because his team had cheated during the final.

urbanisation.meaning: Over the last century, town after town has grown bigger as families leave the farms and settle in built-up areas.
urbanisation.clue: Houses are springing up on the fields, as people leave the villages and urbanisation spreads across our county.

usurp.meaning: Getting hold of a role, a title or a power that really belongs to somebody else.
usurp.clue: The ambitious duke tried to usurp the throne while the young king was still a boy.

utterance.meaning: An utterance is a single thing that someone says, especially one that matters.
utterance.clue: One careless utterance about a pupil's family caused the head teacher to write to her parents that afternoon.

vacant.meaning: If a room is vacant, nobody is in it and it is ready for whoever needs it.
vacant.clue: The caretaker unlocked the vacant classroom so that our club could have somewhere to meet after lunch.

vacillate.meaning: If you go back and forth between two choices, you cannot make your mind up.
vacillate.clue: He began to vacillate about entering the poetry competition, asking his best friend for advice four times.

vacuous.meaning: When an idea is vacuous, it sounds grand but really says nothing at all.
vacuous.clue: The school assembly on healthy eating was vacuous, because nobody could remember a single fact after it.

vague.meaning: A vague description leaves out the details, so you cannot picture what someone is talking about.
vague.clue: His vague answer about where the lost jumper was left did not help the class at all.

valid.meaning: An argument or a reason is valid when it is based on truth and can be trusted.
valid.clue: The examiner accepted her argument as valid, because she had checked every figure twice.

vapid.meaning: A vapid remark has no sparkle in it, and after it nobody has learnt anything new.
vapid.clue: The head's speech about litter was vapid, and even the youngest pupils began to fidget.

vast.meaning: If something is vast, it covers such a large area that you could walk for days without reaching the end.
vast.clue: The vast library at the top of the hill holds thousands of books in rows as long as a street.

venerable.meaning: Somebody venerable is someone we all respect because they have lived such a long time.
venerable.clue: The venerable headmaster, who taught at the school for fifty years, was greeted by the whole school.

ventilation.meaning: Having air moving freely through a room keeps people comfortable, even when it is warm outside.
ventilation.clue: The windows in our classroom stay open all day because the ventilation in this old building is poor.

veracity.meaning: Veracity matters in history books, because the writer must not make anything up.
veracity.clue: Mr Patel checked the veracity of the story before our class printed it in the school newspaper.

verbose.meaning: Being verbose means talking at length about something that needed only a sentence.
verbose.clue: His verbose answer to an easy question filled half a page of our class booklet.

verify.meaning: To test something carefully, so that you know for certain that it is accurate.
verify.clue: The head teacher asked us to verify the total on the sheet before the results went out.

veritable.meaning: Used before a noun to stress that the thing really is what everybody says it is.
veritable.clue: The museum guide told us the dinosaur skeleton was a veritable treasure, and we could hardly walk away.

vernacular.meaning: Words of a region or community used in daily speech, rather than in books or official writing.
vernacular.clue: In our English lesson we heard the vernacular of the north, with words the examiner had never met.

versatile.meaning: If someone is versatile, they can turn their hand to many different subjects or jobs.
versatile.clue: Our versatile caretaker mends dripping taps, fixes the boiler and coaches the school athletics team.

vessel.meaning: A vessel is a large boat or ship, though the word can also mean a hollow container holding a liquid, such as a bottle.
vessel.clue: The museum's model of an old trading vessel sits beside the harbour, and the label explains its long voyage.

viable.meaning: If a plan is viable, it could really be carried out and would probably succeed.
viable.clue: The head teacher said the plan to run a homework club was viable, so the trial will begin next term.

vicinity.meaning: Vicinity means the streets and buildings that lie all around a place you are standing.
vicinity.clue: Our school trip to the science museum will take us into the historic vicinity of the old cathedral.

vigilant.meaning: A vigilant person keeps their attention fixed on what is happening and is quick to spot danger.
vigilant.clue: Two vigilant parents stood at the gate, counting children as they came out of the swimming pool.

vigorously.meaning: To do something vigorously is to do it with lots of energy and physical effort.
vigorously.clue: Our team practised vigorously all term, and on race day they sprinted to the finish line exhausted.

vigour.meaning: Vigour is the power and bounce that a person or animal has in their body.
vigour.clue: Despite the terrible weather, the young foals ran across the field with astonishing vigour.

vilify.meaning: To vilify a person is to describe them in the nastiest possible way so that others think badly of them.
vilify.clue: The newspaper was accused of trying to vilify the young cyclist after he refused to say sorry.

vindicate.meaning: Vindicating somebody means proving publicly that the accusations against them were completely wrong.
vindicate.clue: The new evidence helped to vindicate the caretaker, who everyone had wrongly suspected for months.

vindictive.meaning: A vindictive person holds on to anger long after a quarrel and wants the other party to suffer.
vindictive.clue: Rather than accept the apology, the vindictive captain banned his rival from the team for a whole season.

visionary.meaning: A visionary is often ridiculed at first, because the changes they hope for are still only an idea.
visionary.clue: Our founder was a true visionary, and the little reading corner she opened is now a whole library.

vitriolic.meaning: A vitriolic remark aims to hurt somebody deeply rather than simply explain or help.
vitriolic.clue: Her vitriolic review of the play was so cruel that the young actors refused to read it.

vivacious.meaning: A vivacious person moves about, talks loudly and makes everyone around them feel cheerful too.
vivacious.clue: The vivacious new girl sang in the corridor, and soon half the class were singing with her.

vivid.meaning: A vivid picture uses strong colours and sharp detail, so you feel as though you were there.
vivid.clue: The artist gave us a vivid description of the storm, so we could hear the wind and smell the sea.

vocation.meaning: Someone's vocation is their chosen trade, the work they feel meant to do for the rest of their life.
vocation.clue: She decided that teaching was her vocation and applied for a training place straight after university.

vociferous.meaning: Being vociferous means speaking in a voice so loud that even the back row is certain how you feel.
vociferous.clue: The vociferous parents pushed their way to the front and interrupted the speaker four times.

voluminous.meaning: A voluminous book runs to hundreds of pages, and a voluminous speech seems to go on for hours.
voluminous.clue: The library's newest novel is so voluminous that even our fastest reader would need a whole term.

voracious.meaning: A voracious appetite means someone always feels hungry, and a voracious reader never stops wanting more books.
voracious.clue: The voracious puppy cleared the whole bowl of leftovers before we reached the kitchen door.

vow.meaning: A vow is a promise you make solemnly, knowing that other people will hold you to it.
vow.clue: At the ceremony the bride made her vow to love and support her husband through everything.

waive.meaning: To waive a right is to make a free choice to give it up, without anyone forcing you.
waive.clue: The school agreed to waive the entrance fee for families who needed help with the trip.

wanton.meaning: A wanton act shows no thought for others or for right and wrong.
wanton.clue: The wanton boy threw stones at the windows and then laughed when the police arrived.

wasteful.meaning: A wasteful habit throws away good materials when they could easily be used again.
wasteful.clue: Our new monitor reminds the cleaners how wasteful it is to leave the taps running.

whimsical.meaning: A whimsical invention has a silly, dreamy charm, and nobody expects it to be of any use.
whimsical.clue: On the wall the artist has drawn a whimsical tower with teacup legs and a smiling cloud.

whining.meaning: Someone who is whining keeps on about small annoyances in a voice nobody finds pleasant.
whining.clue: After ten minutes of whining about the cold, the class finally decided to shut the window.

wilful.meaning: A wilful child carries on doing exactly what it wants after being asked several times to stop.
wilful.clue: Despite three warnings from the head, the wilful boy kept pushing his chair during the assembly.

willpower.meaning: Willpower is the inner strength that keeps a person going when giving up would be easier.
willpower.clue: It took real willpower to ignore her phone and finish the last question before the bell.

winsome.meaning: A winsome smile or manner makes people feel warmly inclined towards somebody.
winsome.clue: The winsome puppy flopped onto the back seat and licked every passenger on the journey home.

wistful.meaning: A wistful expression shows a person gently dreaming about somebody or something they have lost.
wistful.clue: He kept staring at the old photographs with a wistful smile, remembering summers at the coast.

woeful.meaning: Someone who is woeful feels in a very miserable state after a loss or a disappointment.
woeful.clue: The team were woeful after the defeat, and their supporters left the ground in silence.

worthy.meaning: A worthy deed is one good enough that people will honestly praise those responsible for it.
worthy.clue: The caretaker was given a certificate for her worthy service to the school over forty years.

wretch.meaning: Calling someone a wretch means you think their life is miserable and deserves real sympathy.
wretch.clue: The old man was a wretch in his last years, and the parish gave him food and a warm room.

yonder.meaning: Yonder is an old-fashioned word people use to point at something far away across fields or water.
yonder.clue: Looking yonder across the lake, we could see the castle tower catching the last of the sun.

zeal.meaning: When a campaigner shows zeal, they do far more than they have to, simply because they care deeply.
zeal.clue: With such zeal for the project, the helpers worked through the holidays to finish the playground.

zenith.meaning: The zenith of someone's life is the period when everything is going as well as it possibly could.
zenith.clue: Her career reached its zenith in the nineties, when she sold records all over Europe.

zephyr.meaning: A zephyr is so mild and gentle that you hardly notice it touching your cheek.
zephyr.clue: A cool zephyr drifted in from the sea, and the runners quickened as they reached the hill.

zestful.meaning: A zestful person approaches every task with sparkle and a readiness to have a go.
zestful.clue: Our zestful guide kept the tour moving, laughing at every question the visitors asked.
